Those readers used to concentrating on humans may feel tempted to skip this chapter, which requires you to attend to nonhuman species. Ironically, this would introduce you to the chapter’s chief conceptual tool. Our categories and discriminations always produce zones of “boredom” and unreadability; powerful projects of categorization, including development and conservation (as well as your scholarly reading practices, whatever they may be), produce persistently uninteresting, invisible, and sometimes illegitimate zones—which I call “gaps.” Universal knowledge projects cannot be understood without attention to gaps. Of course, I would like to entice you to go on despite this warning. I have assumed no technical background. Drawing on what I hope is the widely accessible charisma of nature writing, I proceed as an appreciative traveler into the simultaneously social and natural landscape of the central Meratus Mountains. Social and natural? The deeper we proceed into that conundrum, the less analytic tools we have to consider it. Thinking past our dearly held notions of the autonomy of human sociality, we must consider the interdependence of species. We must turn to the beasts and flowers, not just as symbols and resources, but as co-residents and collaborators.

习惯于关注人类的读者，可能会忍不住跳过这一章，因为它要求你关注非人类物种。讽刺的是，这反而会让你接触本章的核心概念工具。我们的分类与区分总是产生“无聊”和不可读的区域；强大的分类工程，包括发展与保护（以及你作为学者的阅读实践，无论那是什么），都会产生持续被视为无趣、不可见、有时甚至不具正当性的区域——我称之为“空白”。不关注空白，就无法理解普遍知识工程。当然，尽管有这个警告，我还是想吸引你继续读下去。我假定读者没有技术背景。我希望自然写作的魅力能为广大读者所感受，并借助这种魅力，以一名怀着欣赏之情的旅行者的身份，进入中梅拉图斯山脉这既是社会又是自然的地景。社会与自然？我们越深入这个难题，可用于思考它的分析工具就越少。我们必须超越关于人类社会性自主的根深蒂固观念，思考物种之间的相互依赖。我们必须转向野兽与花朵，不仅把它们当作象征和资源，也当作共同居民与合作者。

What do the creatures that make noises in the night say? According to poet Kristiandi Tanumihardja (1994), mainly, we don’t know. In his poem, we hear them speaking, but we can’t understand what they say. But we make a fair and generous guess if, among the many things they say, we imagine them telling us “Don’t bother us; we want to live” (line 25). “Preserve us [lestarikanlah kami],” the poet adds in the next line, speaking for them, and using the word for environmental protection.
夜间发出声响的生物在说什么？诗人克里斯蒂安迪·塔努米哈贾（1994）认为，主要是我们不知道。在他的诗里，我们听见它们说话，却听不懂它们说什么。但如果在它们所说的许多话中，我们想象它们在告诉我们“别打扰我们，我们想活下去”（第25行），那便是一个公正而慷慨的猜测。诗人在下一行替它们加上：“保护我们［lestarikanlah kami］”，用的正是环境保护的词。

International conservationists, and particularly conservation biologists, the scientists most concerned with species preservation, have made this same inference about how to know the interests of nonhuman species. There is a lot we may never know about the motivation and behavior of nonhuman organisms, but we can imagine that they, like us, want to live. In this spirit conservation biologists interpret animal habits and plant growth patterns as species-specific modes of advantage for reproduction and survival. When the urge to live is all we know, we must interpret everything we learn in a calculus of population dynamics and interspecies competition. Meanwhile, the hope of this science is that even such limited understanding might bring us closer to knowing how to live in a multispecies world.

国际保护主义者，尤其是保护生物学家——最关心物种保存的科学家——也作出了同样的推断，以理解非人类物种的利益。关于非人类有机体的动机与行为，有很多我们也许永远无法得知，但我们可以想象，它们像我们一样想活下去。本着这种精神，保护生物学家把动物习性和植物生长模式解释为物种特有的繁殖与生存优势方式。当我们只知道求生的冲动时，就必须把所学到的一切放入种群动态与种间竞争的计算中。同时，这门科学的希望在于，即使是如此有限的理解，也可能让我们更接近懂得如何在一个多物种世界中生活。

In the process of mastering such ways of translating nonhuman lives, most conservation biologists simplify what they know—or what they could know—about humans. Throwing out the libraries on history and culture, they treat humans, like nonhuman species, as a homogeneous group in which every example of behavior merely tells us, “We want to live.” Furthermore, this singular, unitary human calculus of reproduction and survival is based on stereotypes about the human condition created by dominant contemporary urban elites of European descent. Through these cultural assumptions, conservation biologists construct portraits in which humans necessarily threaten the existence of all species that they do not either domesticate or cordon off in preserves.

在掌握这种转译非人类生命的方式的过程中，大多数保护生物学家简化了他们对人类所知——或可能知道——的东西。他们丢开历史与文化的全部书库，像对待非人类物种一样，把人类当作一个同质群体，其中每一个行为范例都只告诉我们：“我们想活下去。”此外，这种单一、统一的人类繁殖与生存计算，建立在当代占主导地位的欧洲裔城市精英所创造的人类境况刻板印象之上。通过这些文化假设，保护生物学家构建出这样的图景：人类必然威胁一切未被他们驯化或圈入保护区的物种的生存。

In opposition to conservationist simplifications of what it means to be human, social scientists have formed a “political ecology.” Political ecology reminds us that human interactions with the environment respond to social conventions and political coercions—not just the pressure of numbers. State regulation and systems of property shape land management.

This seems completely right. However, it is still difficult to understand the diversity of human-nonhuman interactions as long as we learn very little about nonhumans. Social scientists extend the kind of simplification and neglect conservation biologists apply to humans to nonhumans. We rarely hear about the lives of plants and animals; we hear only how they enter human plans. We tap into literatures on symbols and meanings, on class and colonialism, on commodification and the penetration of capitalism. But these literatures do little to help us understand nature: its diversity, its power and constraints, or its multifaceted ways of entering human histories.
为了反对保护主义者对何为人类的简化理解，社会科学家形成了“政治生态学”。政治生态学提醒我们，人类与环境的互动回应社会惯例和政治强制——而不只是人口数量的压力。国家监管与财产制度塑造土地管理。
这看起来完全正确。然而，只要我们对非人类所知甚少，就仍然难以理解人类—非人类互动的多样性。社会科学家把保护生物学家对人类所施加的那类简化和忽视，扩展到非人类身上。我们很少听到植物与动物的生活；我们只听到它们如何进入人类的计划。我们利用关于象征与意义、阶级与殖民主义、商品化与资本主义渗透的文献。但这些文献对我们理解自然帮助不大：它的多样性、它的力量与限制，或它进入人类历史的多种方式。

Since each aims to influence public opinion, it is particularly ironic that environmental social science and biology tend to speak entirely past each other. Each field creates separate conventions of reading; it is difficult to take both into account. We lose a lot in this missed communication. In particular, we lose the ability to look at the intricacies of human relationships to nonhuman species. Conservation biologists segregate nonhumans; political ecologists too often take them for granted as resources for human use. Instead, we might want to look at how species and populations slip in and out of markets, in and out of cultural attention, and in and out of a whole spectrum of not-yet-fully-described interactions between humans and nonhumans. In addressing conservation, this process of description could take us farther than the hackneyed dichotomy between use and preservation: We could study the historical and cultural variety of relations between people, plants, and animals.

由于两者都旨在影响公众舆论，环境社会科学与生物学往往完全彼此错过，这尤其具有讽刺意味。每个领域都创造各自的阅读惯例；很难同时兼顾两者。在这种错过的沟通中，我们损失很多。特别是，我们失去审视人类与非人类物种关系之复杂细节的能力。保护生物学家隔离非人类；政治生态学家则常常把它们视为人类使用的资源，认为理所当然。相反，我们也许想看看物种和种群如何进出市场、进出文化关注，以及进出人类与非人类之间一整个尚未得到充分描述的互动谱系。在处理保护问题时，这一描述过程可能比老套的“利用与保存”二分法带我们走得更远：我们可以研究人、植物和动物之间关系的历史与文化多样性。

One way to a more nuanced account of interactions between human and nonhuman species is to take the landscape as an object of analysis. By landscape I am referring to the configuration of humans and nonhumans across a terrain. I am interested in the material as well as the representational practices of making and maintaining the landscape. The landscape is both “social” (created within human projects) and “natural” (outside of human control; populated by nonhuman species). My emphasis on social-natural landscapes differentiates my analysis from scholars who use “landscape” to refer either to aesthetic conventions, studied apart from a particular terrain, or to the sheer physical arrangement of things, studied without attention to social and cultural programs.

更细致地叙述人类与非人类物种互动的一种方式，是把地景当作分析对象。所谓地景，我指的是人类与非人类在一片地形上的配置。我感兴趣的是制造与维持地景的物质实践和表征实践。地景既是“社会的”（在人类项目中创造），又是“自然的”（在人类控制之外；由非人类物种栖居）。我对社会—自然地景的强调，使我的分析区别于那些把“地景”用于审美惯例（脱离特定地形来研究），或用于事物纯粹物理排列（研究时不关注社会与文化方案）的学者。

Let me turn to a particular social-natural landscape: the central Meratus Mountains as I came to know it in the 1980s and 1990s. Here scattered bamboo houses sat by small swidden fields surrounded by forest regrowth mixing into big forest. The forest here was not primeval but rather “anthropogenic,” human-made forest; however, it was not nearly so neatly managed as the orchards and plantations that this term often describes. When most visitors from the city, including conservation advocates, visited, they saw “natural” forest; and that was how the area was always mapped. Indeed, there was considerable old-growth forest here, but this was mixed with oldgrowth-enriched old orchard-forest as well as patches of younger forest, cycled with fields. This was a weedy, patchwork naturalness without clearly demarcated forest reserves. Weeds have been of little interest to conservationists; we think of them only as indicators of disturbance. Yet this kind of weedy, mixed forest landscape harbors a significant portion of the biodiversity we associate with the tropics. Much of the island of Borneo has been covered with this kind of human-modified rainforest, at least before timber corporations cut it and plantation corporations burned it to replace it with monocrops. To move beyond timber and plantation models in understanding human relations with forests, this weedy forest landscape offers a good deal of insight.

让我转向一个特定的社会—自然地景：我在20世纪80和90年代逐渐了解的中梅拉图斯山脉。在这里，散落的竹屋坐落在小片刀耕火种田旁，周围是混入大森林的次生林。这里的森林并非原始林，而是“人为的”、人造的森林；不过，它远没有这个词常描述的果园和种植园那样整齐管理。大多数来自城市的访客，包括保护倡导者，来访时看到的都是“自然”森林；这个地区也一直是这样被绘制成图的。确实，这里有相当多老龄林，但它与富含老龄树的老果园林混杂，也夹杂着与田地轮作的较年轻森林斑块。这是一种杂草丛生、拼布式的自然性，没有界限分明的森林保护区。杂草很少引起保护主义者的兴趣；我们只把它们当作干扰的指示。然而，这种杂草混杂的森林地景，承载着我们与热带联系在一起的大量生物多样性。婆罗洲岛的大部分地区，至少在被木材公司砍伐、被种植园公司烧毁以换成单一作物之前，曾覆盖着这种经人类改造的热带雨林。要在理解人与森林的关系时超越木材与种植园模式，这种杂草森林地景提供了很多洞见。

Social life in the mountains has also been thought of as “weedy.” The people of the mountains, whom I call Meratus Dayaks, are regionally known as orang bukit, “hill people,” or, one might say, hillbillies. The association of the people and the hills has all the connotations of backward, awkward, derivative, and badly grasped culture that the term hillbilly carries in U.S. English. Meratus Dayaks are regarded as the disorderly cousins of the civilized people in surrounding plains and towns. These are people whose distinctiveness has everything to do with staying out of the way: evading government authority in its various forms; evading soldiers in their continual wars and raids; evading world religion since the spread of Islam in the sixteenth century. It would be easy to ignore them in a study that looked only for the indigenous wisdom of isolated tribes; they are not isolated, only exoticized and despised. It is not tempting to search here for some unique cosmology of nature. Instead, the practical relations of people and forest can tell us about the making of complex landscapes in which humans and diverse nonhumans share space without clear demarcations of separate spheres.

山中的社会生活也曾被视为“杂草式的”。山中的居民——我称他们为梅拉图斯达雅克人——在区域上被称为 orang bukit，“山地人”，或者可以说，乡巴佬。人群与山丘的关联，带有美国英语中 hillbilly 一词所承载的全部含义：文化落后、笨拙、依样仿效却又不得要领。梅拉图斯达雅克人被视为周围平原与城镇文明人的无序表亲。这些人的独特性，完全在于他们懂得避让：躲避各种形式的政府权威；躲避持续战争与突袭中的士兵；自16世纪伊斯兰教传播以来躲避世界宗教。如果一项研究只寻找孤立部落的土著智慧，就很容易忽视他们；他们并不孤立，只是被异域化和蔑视。在这里寻找某种独特的自然宇宙论并不诱人。相反，人与森林的实际关系可以告诉我们，复杂地景是如何形成的；在这些地景中，人类与多样的非人类共享空间，却没有清晰划分的独立领域。

The distinctive feature of the central Meratus landscape has been its confusion of zones of livelihood and zones of forest protection. The forest has been a social and productive space as well as a place for species diversity. Nor is this confusion a site of scarcity: this landscape is rich for livelihood and for species. Yet conservation and development vocabularies make it difficult to describe the central Meratus landscape without a great deal of selfconsciousness. Both conservation and development take the importance of the proper demarcation of spheres of humans and nonhumans, culture and nature, as a given. It seems “natural” to the experts to assume that a good livelihood requires permanent fields just as a healthy forest requires permanent reserves. They would have us see both nature and culture in the Meratus Mountains as a weedy social-ecological roadside. Such edges are the least interesting ecologies and societies as long as we are looking for cleanly demarcated communities of plants or of people. We see only degraded spaces: weeds and hillbillies. But what if we were to turn our perspective to give careful attention to the making of this species-diverse but social landscape?

中梅拉图斯地景的独特特征，是生计区域与森林保护区域的混淆。森林既是社会性的生产空间，也是物种多样性的场所。这种混淆也不是稀缺之地：这片地景在生计和物种两方面都很丰富。然而，保护与发展的词汇让人很难不带强烈自我意识地描述中梅拉图斯地景。保护与发展都把正确划分人类与非人类、文化与自然的领域视为理所当然。对专家来说，假设良好生计需要永久农田，正如健康森林需要永久保护区，似乎是“自然的”。他们希望我们把梅拉图斯山脉的自然与文化都看作杂草丛生的社会—生态路边。只要我们寻找划分清楚的植物群落或人群，这样的边缘就是最无趣的生态与社会。我们只看到退化空间：杂草与乡巴佬。但如果我们转换视角，仔细关注这个物种多样却具有社会性的地景是如何形成的，会怎样？

This turn of perspective shifts us into what I call “gaps.” Gaps are conceptual spaces and real places into which powerful demarcations do not travel well. The gaps of the central Meratus landscape call attention to the bad transportability of demarcations of human livelihood versus nature conservation, productive farms versus forest reserves, and settled culture versus the wild, as each of these keeps us from appreciating the history of socialnatural landscapes.
这种视角转换把我们带入我所谓的“空白”。空白是强大的划分难以通行的概念空间和真实地点。中梅拉图斯地景的空白，让人注意到人类生计与自然保护、生产性农场与森林保护区、定居文化与荒野等划分的糟糕可移植性，因为每一项都妨碍我们欣赏社会—自然地景的历史。
By taking on these categories, I find myself in dialogue with a generation of symbolic and ecological anthropologists who argue that various indigenous people do not believe in these categories.

But that is not my point, although it may also be partially true. These categories do not organize the landscape materially. If we release ourselves from their hegemony, we can explore how interactions among humans and nonhumans on this landscape create its patches and trajectories. We can follow how the forest becomes readable as a social space. We can make sense, too, of Meratus respect for these authoritative conservation and development demarcations, but as the rhetoric of leaders assuaging powerful outsiders, rather than as the practice of daily life. It is not that Meratus never heard of these categories; they have known them for a long time. But in the central mountains they have put them in a particular, ceremonial place for community leaders. With this placement, the categories are crippled in their mode of traveling; they organize expert ways of seeing but not the landscapes that grow up in their gaps.
在质疑这些范畴时，我发现自己是在与一代象征人类学家和生态人类学家对话；他们论证各种土著民族并不相信这些范畴。

但这不是我的观点，尽管它可能也部分正确。这些范畴并没有在物质上组织地景。如果我们从它们的主导中解放出来，就能探索这片地景上人类与非人类的互动如何创造其斑块与轨迹。我们可以追踪森林如何变得可读为一个社会空间。我们也可以理解梅拉图斯人对这些权威性保护与发展划分的尊重，但那是领袖安抚强大外来者的修辞，而不是日常生活的实践。并不是梅拉图斯人从未听说过这些范畴；他们已经认识它们很久了。但在中部山区，他们把这些范畴放在一个特殊的、仪式性的位置，留给社区领袖。经过这样的安置，这些范畴在传播方式上就失效了；它们组织专家的观看方式，却不组织在其空白中生长起来的地景。

A consideration of gaps turns us from a quick dismissal of weedy, hillbilly edges to explore species-rich landscapes in which human livelihood maintains forests. This switch in perspective does not convert the forests into pristine old-growth or the people into mysterious primitives; they maintain their weedy, hillbilly features. However, through the switch we can see the richness and complexity of the history of weediness, as well as the limitations of categories that are imagined to be universals that travel everywhere. And so I organize my description in the spaces these categories make unimaginable, that is, their gaps. The challenge in making this natural-social landscape come to life on paper is to give the nonhuman species as much liveliness as the humans. As in the poem with which I began, I do my best to offer sounds and words to forest creatures. I use the ethnographic present to honor the long timescale in which this landscape was assembled, and in the hope that as I write today it has not been totally dismantled by the frontiermaking dynamics I came to know in other Meratus areas in the 1990s.

对空白的思考，使我们不再匆匆贬低杂草丛生、乡巴佬式的边缘，而去探索人类生计维持森林的物种丰富地景。这种视角转换不会把森林变成原始老龄林，也不会把人变成神秘原始人；他们仍保留杂草式、乡巴佬式的特征。然而，通过这种转换，我们可以看到杂草性历史的丰富与复杂，也可以看到那些被想象为放之四海而皆准的普遍范畴的局限。因此，我把描述组织在这些范畴无法想象的空间中，也就是它们的空白里。让这个自然—社会地景在纸上生动起来，挑战在于给予非人类物种与人类同样多的生气。正如我开头那首诗，我尽力为森林生物提供声音和词语。我使用民族志现在时，是为了尊重这片地景被组装起来的漫长时间尺度，也希望在我今天写作时，它尚未被我在20世纪90年代其他梅拉图斯地区所了解的边疆制造动力完全拆解。
Inside the Gap between Cultivated and Wild
在栽培与野生之间的空白内部

It is fruit season. A dry spell after the heavy monsoon rains has stimulated flowering, and the fruits have come in, luscious and plentiful. Turn their names over in your mouth: durian, lahung, langsat, rambutan, maritam, buku-buku, rambai, manggu, tiwadak, kulidang.... When the fruits ripen en masse, we can eat as much as we want.

现在是水果季节。季风大雨后的一段干旱刺激了开花，果实随之而来，甘美而丰盛。把它们的名字在嘴里翻来覆去：榴莲（durian）、拉洪（lahung）、兰撒（langsat）、红毛丹（rambutan）、马里坦（maritam）、布库布库（buku-buku）、兰拜（rambai）、芒古（manggu）、蒂瓦达克（tiwadak）、库利当（kulidang）……当果实一齐成熟时，我们可以想吃多少就吃多少。

The fruits we picked this morning are in a basket at the front of the house, where passing visitors, seeing us through the door, can come up to share them with us. In fruit season, everyone is generous with fruits: please take some home. But before that we can sit and chat and refresh ourselves with fruit. And as we eat we throw the seeds out the door into the brush surrounding the isolated house.
我们今早摘的果实放在屋前的篮子里。路过的访客透过门看到我们，可以上来与我们分享。水果季节里，人人对水果都很慷慨：请带些回家。但在此之前，我们可以坐着聊天，用水果提神。我们一边吃，一边把种子从门口扔进环绕这座孤立屋子的灌木丛。

The seeds of many tropical fruits sprout best when allowed to grow immediately. The temperate plants that probably come to mind for most of my readers—apples, peaches—require a dormancy period, a winter perhaps, before they will sprout and grow. Not so for many tropical fruits. If you keep the seeds for more than a few days before sprouting them, they will die. But seeds thrown out the door of the house often sprout and grow.
许多热带水果的种子，在能立即生长时发芽最好。我的大多数读者可能想到的温带植物——苹果、桃子——需要一段休眠期，也许要经历一个冬天，才会发芽生长。许多热带水果则不然。如果你把种子留上好几天才发芽，它们就会死。但从屋门扔出去的种子常常发芽生长。

A year or two later the household will have moved on. The bamboo and thatch and bark of the house decay quickly. If the houseposts are made of sungkai (Peronema canescens), they may have sprouted and become new, quick-growing secondary forest trees. Within a few years, it would be hard for a stranger to know that a house had been there. Yet there is a grove of fruit trees gathered together near this spot. These are the trees we “planted” by throwing their seeds out the door. The faster growing, smaller species will begin to bear fruit in five or six years. In those same years, what once was a swidden field around the house will have become a shady young forest with trees the diameter of one’s arm. The fruits whose seeds we deposited will be growing amidst a large variety of self-propagating herbs and trees. The fruit trees will mature as part of a forest. And while many of my temperate-climate readers may have passed a few apple trees in regrowing temperate forest and imagined an old homestead, few have experienced a landscape in which all the fruits one enjoys—planted or self-propagating—are an integral part of the forest. There are no dedicated orchards in the central Meratus Mountains; all fruit trees there must be able to survive in the forest, whether the species evolved in this area or was transported from elsewhere, and whether the individual was planted or grew without human intervention.

一两年后，这户人家会搬走。竹、茅草和树皮建成的房子很快朽坏。如果房柱是 sungkai（Peronema canescens）木做的，它们可能已经发芽，长成新的、速生的次生林树木。几年之内，陌生人就很难知道这里曾有过一座房子。然而，在这附近却聚集成一片果树。这些就是我们“种下”的树，方式是把种子扔出门外。生长较快的较小树种五六年内就会开始结果。同样这几年里，房子周围曾经的刀耕火种田，会变成一片有臂膀粗细树木的阴凉幼林。我们播下种子的果树，将在各种各样自生自长的草本植物和树木之间生长。果树将作为森林的一部分成熟。我的许多温带气候读者也许在再生温带森林中见过几棵苹果树，并想象出一处旧宅；但很少有人经历过这样的地景：所有令人享受的果实——无论是栽种的还是自生的——都是森林的组成部分。中梅拉图斯山脉没有专门的果园；那里所有果树都必须在森林中存活，无论该物种是在此地演化还是从别处传来，也无论植株是人工栽种还是不经人类干预而生长。

The image of casually propagated fruit trees in the forest opens a way to explore a landscape in which an important number of plants fall between familiar categories of “cultivated” and “wild.” These categories are the starting line for all of us who care about biodiversity protection. Since we know best the landscape of capitalist agriculture, it makes perfect sense to draw a hard line between the domestic or cultivated, whose populations rise and fall depending on the market, and the wild, so often casually destroyed without regard to future populations. Humans are already responsible for domestic populations. In contrast, environmental movements and environmental science have formed over concerns about wild things, and we think of these as the “biodiversity” we hope to protect. Yet what of landscapes in which significant numbers of organisms are neither properly domestic and cultivated nor wild and independent from human nurture and propagation? Might these require new approaches to biodiversity conservation? And, indeed, to conceptualizing nature in a global perspective?

随意繁衍的果树置身森林这一意象，开辟了一条道路，去探索一种地景：其中相当数量的植物落在“栽培”与“野生”这两个熟悉范畴之间。这些范畴是我们所有关心生物多样性保护的人的起跑线。由于我们最了解资本主义农业的地景，因此在驯化或栽培的种群（其数量随市场起伏）与野生的种群（常常被随意毁灭，不顾未来种群）之间划出一条硬线，显得完全合理。人类已经对驯化种群负有责任。相比之下，环境运动和环境科学是围绕对野生之物的关切形成的，我们把它们视为希望保护的“生物多样性”。然而，对于那些大量生物既非真正驯化栽培、也非野生独立于人类培育与繁殖的地景，又当如何？它们是否需要生物多样性保护的新方法？以及，是否需要以全球视角重新概念化自然？

Anthropologists who are asked about these kinds of questions usually turn first to the ideas of the inhabitants. Do Meratus Dayaks have categories of “cultivated” and “wild”? they inquire. This is an important question, for the nonhumans as well as the humans, because humans so often organize their interspecies practices in relation to their cultural categories. So let me begin here: Meratus distinguish between “planted plants” (tanaman) and plants that “grow themselves” (tumbuh sa’urang). I’ve followed the Meratus idiom above to speak of “self-propagating herbs and trees” although nonhuman animals, wind, and other agents may be required to propagate these plants. Yet it seems a useful enough way to distinguish the human-planted and the merely human-encountered herb or tree.

被问到这类问题时，人类学家通常首先转向当地居民的观念。他们会问：梅拉图斯达雅克人是否有“栽培”与“野生”的范畴？这个问题很重要，无论对非人类还是人类而言，因为人类常常依据其文化范畴来组织跨物种实践。那么让我从这里开始：梅拉图斯人区分“栽种的植物”（tanaman）和“自己生长的植物”（tumbuh sa'urang）。我在上文遵循梅拉图斯的说法，谈到“自生自长的草本植物和树木”，尽管可能需要非人类动物、风和其他动因来传播这些植物。不过，这似乎是区分人类栽种与人仅仅遇到的草木的一个足够有用的方式。

The Meratus distinction does not, however, distinguish between species as uniform blocks. The individuals of many species may either be planted or grow themselves; the distinction describes the practice, not the species characteristic. Different forms of planting are recognized, ranging from the deliberate burying of seeds to the more casual sprouting of a rubbish heap. Furthermore, there are many human practices other than planting that are recognized as encouraging particular plants. Some self-propagating plants, such as rattans and wild gingers, do well sprouting in the light gap of a swidden. Some, such as bamboos, are not destroyed by swidden making and flourish with new advantage in the regrowing forest. Others, such as honey bee-friendly trees, are saved when swiddens are cleared. Choking weeds, vines, and parasites are removed around some trees to maintain them. Meratus recognize this continuum of human practices involved in encouraging plant growth. While this attention to specific practices, rather than species classes, does not solve the problem of conservation in the Meratus Mountains, it is a good beginning for opening up preconceived frameworks to investigate forms of interaction between humans and plants.

然而，梅拉图斯的区分并不把物种当作统一的块体来区分。许多物种的个体既可能被栽种，也可能自己生长；这一区分描述的是实践，而不是物种特征。他们承认不同的栽种形式，从刻意埋下种子，到垃圾堆里更为随意的发芽。此外，除栽种之外，还有许多人类实践被认为能促进特定植物。有些自生植物，如棕榈藤与野姜，在刀耕火种田的光隙中发芽良好。有些如竹子，不会因刀耕火种而毁灭，反而在再生林中以新的优势繁茂。另一些如对蜜蜂友好的树，在清理刀耕火种田时会被保留。人们会在一些树周围清除缠绕的杂草、藤蔓和寄生植物，以维护它们。梅拉图斯人承认这一系列促进植物生长的人类实践连续统。虽然关注具体实践而非物种类别，并不能解决梅拉图斯山脉的保护问题，但它是打开先入为主的框架、探究人类与植物互动形式的一个良好开端。

Let me return to fruits. City people expect a wide variety of fruits, generated from importing fruits from around the world and by creating new variety through breeding. There are additional sources of variety in the central Meratus Mountains. The forest of the Meratus Mountains is biologically diverse; Borneo is a center of tropical fruit diversity. Most fruits that are even partially cultivated have close cousins within the Bornean forest. This variety is much enjoyed by humans and other animals. Like orangutans, civets, wild pigs, and bats, humans have become one of the ways fruit trees, in all their variety, distribute their seeds. Fruit tree biodiversity is maintained in part by those human-fruit tree interactions that fall somewhere in the gap between cultivation and the wild.

让我回到水果。城市人期待种类繁多的水果，这来自从世界各地进口水果，也来自通过育种创造新品种。中梅拉图斯山脉还有额外的多样性来源。梅拉图斯山脉的森林在生物上多样；婆罗洲是热带水果多样性的中心。即使只是部分栽培的水果，大多数在婆罗洲森林里都有近亲。这种多样性深受人类和其他动物喜爱。与猩猩、麝猫、野猪和蝙蝠一样，人类已成为果树——在其全部多样性中——传播种子的方式之一。果树生物多样性，部分由那些落在栽培与野生之间空白某处的人类—果树互动来维持。

The most famous fruit of the Bornean rainforest is the durian. The ripe fruit is green and spikey and as large as an American football; inside the thick skin are the foul and fine smelling, custardy seed coverings that comprise the valued fruit. The naturalist Alfred Wallace (1962: 57) wrote: “Its consistence and flavour are undescribable. A rich butter-like custard highly flavoured with almonds gives the best general idea of it, but intermingled with it come wafts of flavour that call to mind cream-cheese, onion-sauce, brown sherry, and other incongruities.”

In the Meratus Mountains, only fruits still hanging on the tree are the exclusive property of tree claimants. While unripe durian makes a wonderful cooked dish, and tree claimants may harvest it, it is the open competition for ripe fallen fruits that captures the most attention in durian season. Teenagers hike through the forest in the middle of the night to search under good trees at dawn’s first light. They bring home baskets of newly fallen durian and pass them around for a drunkenly rich breakfast.
婆罗洲雨林最著名的水果是榴莲。成熟的果实绿色、带刺，像美式橄榄球那么大；厚皮下是气味既臭又妙、奶油冻状的种衣，构成受人珍视的果肉。博物学家阿尔弗雷德·华莱士（1962: 57）写道：“其质地与风味难以描述。浓郁如黄油、带有浓烈杏仁味的蛋奶冻，最能给人一个大致的印象，但其中交织着阵阵气味，令人想起奶油奶酪、洋葱酱、棕色雪利酒以及其他不协调之物。”
在梅拉图斯山脉，只有仍挂在树上的果实才归树木认领者专有。未熟榴莲是绝佳的熟食，树木认领者可以采收；但榴莲季最引人注目的，是对成熟落果的公开竞争。少年们在半夜徒步穿过森林，在黎明第一缕光下到好树下搜寻。他们带回家一篮篮刚掉落的榴莲，传递分享，作为一顿醉人的丰盛早餐。

Durian is thought to have evolved in Borneo: certainly, it flourishes in the forest there. In a good fruit season, one can see dozens of durian seedlings growing up all around a tree, where the sated eaters, human or nonhuman, have discarded the seeds. Not many of them survive in that deep shade; but others, transported elsewhere, may have a better chance. That includes those that are carefully planted and tended. It also includes those that grow from refuse heaps and casual droppings.
榴莲被认为是在婆罗洲演化出来的：它当然在那里森林中繁茂生长。在好年景的果季，人们能看到一棵树周围长出几十株榴莲幼苗，那是吃饱的食客——人或非人——丢弃种子之处。它们中没有多少能在浓荫下存活；但另一些被带到别处的种子，可能有更好的机会。这包括被仔细栽种和照料的幼苗，也包括从垃圾堆或随手丢落的种子中长出的幼苗。
Durian is such a well-loved fruit that most trees in the Meratus Mountains are claimed. Those who plant a tree, and their descendants, claim it.

Those who find a self-seeding tree and watch and nurture it can also claim it. Trees can also become unclaimed, usually when the claimants leave the area and stop paying enough attention to the tree to know its uneven fruiting schedule. In this state, another person can claim the tree, or neighbors who know and watch it may share its fruits. It would be rare to kill a durian tree in swidden-making; the person who killed one would have to pay a large fine to the tree’s claimants. Through a combination of distributing, planting, tending, and saving trees, Meratus increase the durian population of the forest.

Durian has a host of close relatives that are also valued for their fruit. The best, to me, is lahung, a deep-red, long-spiked globe that resembles a giant sea urchin. Lahung is somewhat less commonly planted than durian, but it is a valued fruit tree of the forest and thus commonly claimed, protected, and carefully watched for its fruiting schedule. In contrast, pampakin, whose bright-orange and intensely sweet arils remind me of the icing of Halloween cupcakes, is a cultivate. It is considered a new durian species for the area. On the other side of the continuum, the small fruited durians, such as “bird’s lahung” (lahung burung), are rarely purposefully planted, although they may be gathered when encountered in a hike in the forest. Durian relatives run a full gamut of cultivated-to-wild options.
榴莲是如此受人喜爱的水果，梅拉图斯山脉的大多数榴莲树都被认领。栽种一棵树的人及其后代认领它。
发现一株自生树、照看并培育它的人也可以认领它。树木也可能变成无主，通常是因为认领者离开该地区，不再足够关注这棵树，以至于不了解它不规则的结实周期。在这种情况下，另一个人可以认领这棵树，或者认识并照看它的邻居可以分享其果实。在刀耕火种中杀死一棵榴莲树会很罕见；杀死树的人必须向树的认领者支付高额罚款。通过传播、栽种、照料和保留树木等做法的结合，梅拉图斯人增加了森林中的榴莲种群。

榴莲有许多近亲，其果实也受人珍视。在我看来最好的是拉洪（lahung），一个深红色、长刺的球体，像巨大的海胆。拉洪的栽种不如榴莲常见，但它是森林中宝贵的果树，因此常被认领、保护，并仔细留意其结实周期。相比之下，帕姆帕金（pampakin）的亮橙色、极甜假种皮让我想起万圣节纸杯蛋糕上的糖霜，它是一种栽培植物。它被视为该地区新出现的榴莲物种。在连续统的另一端，小果榴莲，如“鸟拉洪”（lahung burung），很少被有意栽种，尽管在森林徒步中遇到时可以采集。榴莲的近亲涵盖从栽培到野生的完整谱系。

Mangos are another diverse group of fruits in the Meratus forest. They range from the sour hambawang, rarely deliberately planted but much enjoyed as a trailside snack, to the strongly scented binjai, mainly known as a planted and tended tree. There are tiny mangos (rawa-rawa) and huge ones (kwini), and they can be bitingly sour (tandoi) or intensely sweet (binjai and kwini are the sweetest, but with completely different tastes). Their diversity is appreciated by Meratus, who enjoy the opportunity to savor their scents and flavors. Similarly, the diversity of litchi-like Nephelium fruits is much appreciated—and encouraged. The red, hairy rambutan, grown in many parts of Southeast Asia, is planted and enjoyed, but alongside its many relatives: the subtler, smaller buku-buku; the juicy siwau; the smooth-skinned ringkit; the biting maritam (I thought of its taste as somewhere between a pineapple and a raspberry); the tiny, oblong jari-jari; and many more. People look forward to these fruits, learn where they grow unnoticed in the woods, claim them; watch their ripening schedules, harvest them in great quantities, and plant them, sometimes casually in refuse heaps, and sometimes purposefully, in the swidden or by the house. In the gap between cultivated and wild, they flourish.

芒果是梅拉图斯森林中另一个多样的水果类群。从很少被有意栽种、却大受喜爱的路边零食酸汉巴旺（hambawang），到主要作为栽种和照料树木而闻名的浓香宾贾伊（binjai）。有小小的拉瓦拉瓦（rawa-rawa）和巨大的奎尼（kwini），有的酸得刺人（坦多伊，tandoi），有的极甜（宾贾伊和奎尼最甜，但味道完全不同）。梅拉图斯人欣赏它们的多样性，享受品味其香气和风味的机会。同样，荔枝般的韶子属水果的多样性也大受欣赏——并得到促进。红色、毛茸茸的红毛丹在东南亚许多地方栽培并受人喜爱，但它还有许多近亲：风味更淡雅、个头更小的布库布库；多汁的西瓦乌（siwau）；表皮光滑的林基特（ringkit）；酸得刺人的马里坦（我觉得其味道介于菠萝和覆盆子之间）；细小、长圆形的贾里贾里（jari-jari）；以及许多其他种类。人们期待这些水果，找出它们在林中不为人注意的生长地点，认领它们，留意其成熟时间，大量采收，并栽种它们——有时随意种在垃圾堆里，有时有意种在刀耕火种田或房屋旁。在栽培与野生之间的空白中，它们繁茂生长。

One of the most important and most diverse groups of fruits of the Meratus forest is the Artocarpus group, whose best known representatives in the English-speaking world are jackfruit and breadfruit. Jackfruit (nangka) and breadfruit (sukun) are known in the Meratus Mountains in cultivation; but both are rather unimportant. A more relevant species is tarap (A. elastica), a great forest tree only rarely deliberately planted because it is rarely in short supply. The bark can be used for cloth; the sticky, milky sap is used for bird lime; and the sweet, yellow seed coverings of the ball-like fruits are eaten, both raw as a snack and cooked as a side dish with rice. Yet tarap is far from the only Artocarpus of the Meratus forest. I remember binturung and kulidang particularly clearly because we ate a lot of them one season when I was living with a family for whom rice supplies were low; we gathered baskets of the immature forest fruits and cooked them for lunch and dinner. We also ate them ripe. These fruits are plentiful enough in the forest and thus rarely deliberately planted. Other Artocarpus are planted, such as tiwadak (A. champeden), whose sweet arils sit in a long, drooping fruit. The variety of Artocarpus fruits spans and confuses the distinction between cultivate and wild.

The range of human-nonhuman interactions that occupy the gap between domesticated and wild is also relevant to animals. Consider pigs: Meratus households sometimes keep a pig. In the central mountains, it is unlikely that the pig will be kept in an enclosure. Instead, the pig is set out in an old swidden field in the process of regrowing into forest. The foraging in the old swidden field is good: There may be sweet potatoes, cassava, taro, bananas and papayas, sugar cane and eggplants; and there are certainly the tender weeds and herbs of the regrowing forest. Meratus told me that the pig is unlikely to stray far from this good foraging, which compares favorably, from a pig’s perspective, to the more open, big forest with its sparse undergrowth. When they need the pig, they told me, they go to the old swidden and find it. Meanwhile, the chances of the pig coming into contact with migrating bearded pigs are good, especially since wild pigs, too, are drawn to old swiddens. People say that the pigs cross-breed; I am unclear what biological differences separate human-raised pigs and forest pigs in the Meratus Mountains. In any case, the rearing of the human-raised pigs involves rearing piglets enough to bond them to people, and then setting them out in good forage. If one ignores the fact that the pigs end up as food, the relationship does not seem that different than that between people and their pet hornbills, who, fed and coddled as babies, come back to visit their old owners between flights across the forest.

占据驯化与野生之间空白的人类—非人类互动，也与动物有关。想想猪：梅拉图斯人的家庭有时养一头猪。在中部山区，猪不太可能被养在圈里。相反，猪被放到一片正在恢复成森林的旧刀耕火种田里。旧田里的觅食条件很好：可能有甘薯、木薯、芋头、香蕉和木瓜、甘蔗和茄子；当然还有再生林中柔嫩的杂草与草本植物。梅拉图斯人告诉我，猪不太可能离开这片良好的觅食地，因为从猪的角度看，它比林下稀疏、更开阔的大森林好得多。他们说，需要猪的时候，就去旧田里找它。与此同时，猪与迁徙的胡须野猪接触的机会很大，尤其是野猪也会被旧刀耕火种田吸引。人们说猪会杂交；我不清楚在梅拉图斯山脉，人养的猪与森林野猪之间有什么生物学差异。无论如何，人养猪包括把小猪养到足以与人建立感情，然后放到好的觅食地。如果忽略猪最终成为食物这一事实，这种关系似乎与人和宠物犀鸟的关系没有太大不同：犀鸟幼时被喂养宠爱，在飞越森林的间隙回来拜访旧主人。
A more environmentally significant relationship of semi-domestication with an animal connects Meratus and giant honey bees, Apis dorsata.

Meratus call this migratory bee indu wanyi, and they rely on it as a source of honey and beeswax. Like European honey bees, indu wanyi build a honey-filled wax comb. Unlike their European cousins, they do not nest inside a closed space; instead, they hang their combs in a well-lighted space under a high tree branch. Unlike European honey bees, they need light to guide each other to foraging spots, and this is why they prefer open places. In the Meratus forest, this means that they build on the branches of the tallest forest trees, those we call “emergent” to mark the way they tower above the next level of the rainforest canopy. The building of combs does not, as far as I can tell, damage the tree in any way. But these trees are often covered with vines and epiphytes, and their architecturally best branches may be blocked by competing smaller growth. Meratus prepare potential honey trees (linub) for the bees, cleaning off competing vegetation. The migratory bees come back again and again, in season, to the prepared trees. Meratus say that bees will not come back to a tree that has not been cared for.
一种在环境上更重要的半驯化动物关系，连接着梅拉图斯人与大蜜蜂（Apis dorsata）。

梅拉图斯人称这种迁徙蜂为 indu wanyi，依赖它获取蜂蜜和蜂蜡。像欧洲蜜蜂一样，indu wanyi 筑充满蜂蜜的蜡巢。与欧洲蜜蜂不同的是，它们不在封闭空间内筑巢；它们把蜂巢悬挂在高树枝下光线充足的空间。与欧洲蜜蜂不同，它们需要光线引导彼此前往觅食点，这就是它们偏爱开阔地方的原因。在梅拉图斯森林中，这意味着它们会把巢筑在最高森林树的枝条上，也就是我们称为“露冠树”的那些高出下一层雨林冠层的树。据我所能判断，筑巢不会以任何方式损害树木。但这些树常常覆盖着藤蔓和附生植物，结构上最好的枝条可能被竞争的较小植物挡住。梅拉图斯人会为蜜蜂准备潜在的蜜树（linub），清除竞争的植被。迁徙蜂会应季一次又一次回到准备好的树上。梅拉图斯人说，蜜蜂不会回到无人照料的树上。

Meratus know which trees make good honey trees. Mangaris, Koompassia excelsa, is the tallest tree of the Bornean rainforest, recorded to grow over 260 feet; it is also the most popular of all trees for the bees, and in many other Dayak languages across Borneo is known by the local word for “honey tree.” Mangaris often host more than fifty colonies in a good bee season. Binuang (Octomeles sumatrana), another huge tree whose circumference may exceed mangaris, is also a good honey tree. So are a number of kinds of damar, the dipterocarps that dominate the Bornean rainforest. Other honey trees of the central mountains include alaran (another dipterocarp), salang’ai, tampuruyung, pulayi (Alstonia sp.), mampiring (Agathis alba), jalamu, hara wilas (Ficus sp.) and occasionally lua’ (Ficus sp.), kupang, mijalungan, kasai (Pometia pinnata), tikus, jalanut, simunan, and anglai. Damar, salang’ai, and jalamu trees often have as many as forty colonies. Binuang and hara wilas may invite fifteen to twenty colonies. Most of the other trees are less good sites, attracting perhaps only three to five colonies at any one time.

梅拉图斯人知道哪些树能成为好蜜树。曼加里斯（mangaris，Koompassia excelsa）是婆罗洲雨林最高的树，记录可长到260英尺以上；它也是所有树木中最受蜜蜂青睐的一种，在婆罗洲许多其他达雅克语言中，它以当地表示“蜜树”的词而闻名。在好蜂季，曼加里斯常常容纳50多个蜂群。比努昂（binuang，Octomeles sumatrana）是另一种巨树，其周长可能超过曼加里斯，也是好蜜树。若干种达玛树（damar）亦然，它们是婆罗洲雨林占优势的龙脑香科树。中部山区的其他蜜树包括 alaran（另一种龙脑香树）、salang'ai、tampuruyung、pulayi（Alstonia sp.）、mampiring（Agathis alba）、jalamu、hara wilas（Ficus sp.），偶尔还有 lua'（Ficus sp.）、kupang、mijalungan、kasai（Pometia pinnata）、tikus、jalanut、simunan 和 anglai。达玛、salang'ai 和 jalamu 树常常多达40个蜂群。比努昂和 hara wilas 可能招来15到20个蜂群。其他大多数树是较差的场所，一次可能只吸引三到五个蜂群。

Meratus claim, prepare, and protect these trees. In a few cases (e.g., the fast-growing binuang), they plant them in old swiddens. Most commonly, a man claims a tree by being the first to clean it, or if the tree has been abandoned by other claimants, by reviving its cleaning. He passes this claim to his children as long as they are active in maintaining the tree as a honey tree. Most women do not climb and clean honey trees; the principal claimants are men. (Sisters retain rights to honey.) A three-species relationship is set up among bees, honey trees, and people. People encourage comb-building by preparing the trees. They save the honey trees from being cut in swiddenmaking and other projects. Although the arrangement may not be equally advantageous for each species, each species comes to depend on it. In neighboring areas in which loggers and plantation developers have cut down most of these tall trees, people report that there is no longer a bee migration. Furthermore, the tree species are in danger. Given the diversity of the forest and the wide spacing between emergents, many of these forest giants are quite isolated, species-wise, in the forest; every emergent tree that is cut down deprives a section of the forest of a source of seed for that species. The saving of honey trees preserves the number and variety of emergents—as well as providing a nesting place for bees. Between cultivation and the wild, bees, honey trees, and humans have created a mutually productive, symbiotic relationship.

梅拉图斯人认领、准备并保护这些树。在少数情况下（例如速生的比努昂），他们会在旧刀耕火种田里栽种它们。最常见的是，一名男子通过第一个清理某棵树来认领它，或者如果这棵树已被其他认领者遗弃，他就通过重新清理来恢复认领。只要子女积极维护这棵树作为蜜树，他就把认领权传给他们。大多数女性不攀爬清理蜜树；主要认领者是男性。（姐妹保留对蜂蜜的权利。）蜜蜂、蜜树和人之间建立起三物种关系。人通过准备树木来鼓励筑巢。他们在刀耕火种和其他项目中保住蜜树不被砍伐。虽然这种安排对每个物种未必同样有利，但每个物种都变得依赖它。在邻近地区，伐木者和种植园开发商砍掉了大部分这样的高大树木，人们报告说蜜蜂迁徙已不再出现。此外，这些树种也处于危险之中。鉴于森林的多样性以及露冠树之间宽阔的间距，这些森林巨人在森林中从物种角度讲相当孤立；每砍掉一棵露冠树，就使一片森林失去该物种的种子来源。保住蜜树，既保护了露冠树的数量和多样性，也为蜜蜂提供了筑巢处。在栽培与野生之间，蜜蜂、蜜树和人创造了一种互惠的生产性共生关系。

They imitated the sawing buzz of the keke, an insect from the forest that sings every day at around four in the afternoon, reminding us of the time. They sang the sweet goodnight note of the lingut, a nocturnal giant millipede that lives in the trees. We tried out the melodic cackle of the haruwai argus pheasant, which crows from its cleared “swidden” on the forest floor. Immersed in the pleasures of this textured local knowledge, it was easy for me to imagine that this was a hidden world, enclosed and lost from the sounds of televisions, chain saws, and freeway traffic. After all, the trope of other cultures and natures as forgotten worlds is so much a part of the way city people are taught to think; we fantasize the beauty of pristine nature and pristine culture only, just as we arrive, threatened by the destruction of the outside world. Yet, for all its big forests and its rich lore the Meratus landscape is not, in any way, a lost world. It is a landscape made by a history of movement and connection. Trade brings both humans and nonhumans in and out of the mountains. Trade in this area is hundreds of years old, indeed, probably as old as human occupation. Antique collectors still comb through the mountains buying up the ancient Chinese plates and engraved brass stools and trays exchanged for Meratus products in earlier times. While some trade is relatively local,

most trade extends outward from the Meratus Mountains, sending rare products to China, Europe, and around the world. Most of this trade concerns forest products: the resins, rubbers, and incense woods of the tropical rainforest, the exotic animal products—python skins, bezoar stones, beeswax, and edible swifts’ nests; durable ironwood shingles and flexible rattan strips; herbs sold as contraceptives and aphrodisiacs; orchids and songbirds and tiny parrots taken live from the forest.

The most amazing thing about this trade is the number of different products it encompasses. Almost all of its products are available only in small quantities, sporadically encountered. The Meratus collector must keep his eyes open for the whole variety of possible products. (I use the masculine “his” because most collectors are men.) The collector must keep his ears open, too, for news of emerging markets for other products. In the 1980s, there was a rage for the gall bladders of bears, used by Korean loggers and their business partners as aphrodisiacs. There has been a growing market for antidotes to sorcery for plainsmen who believe themselves the victims of mountain magic: the hair of albino deer; oil in which particular bird feathers or insects have been soaked. Marketable incense resins come in different kinds: the diseased heart of garu aloes wood; fragrant dahupa and manyan benzoin; kaladan camphor. Aromatic barks (e.g., sintuk) also find small markets. Nonaromatic resins are sometimes on the market, sometimes off: the damar resins of the great emergent dipterocarp trees, classified commercially as “white,” “black,” “cat’s eye,” “stone,” etc.; the copal resin of the mountain conifer, mampiring.

While synthetic resins have replaced these in most of their international industrial uses, they still have specialized market niches, as well as being used at home. Furthermore, some kinds of collecting require the gatherer to bring together many scattered plants, whether of the same or complementary species; blowpipe poison, for example, is called ratusan, “hundreds,” to acknowledge the large number of ipuh trees (Antiaris toxicana and others) whose latex is combined to produce the poison.

Commercial collecting of forest products requires a sharp eye for plant and animal diversity and for the particularity of sites and ecological niches in the forest.
