This argument runs against stereotypes of indigenous knowledge; the more detailed a community’s knowledge of the forest, the more it is assumed that they have no contact with the surrounding world. Yet the forest-products’ trade creates sharp-eyed collectors, eager to recognize new species. It is also true that commercialization can ruin the forest quickly. As I described in chapter 1, the east-side forest was turned into a free-for-all of destruction in the 1990s. Knowledgeable Meratus collectors joined clueless outsiders in the rush to plunder the landscape before the imagined end. In this context, it was easy to see that the same sharp eyes and ears, attuned to market rumors and the opportunities of forest diversity, could turn to join frontier-style destruction or to enhance long-term forest maintenance. What accounts for the difference?

林产品的商业采集需要敏锐的眼光，去辨识动植物多样性，以及森林中地点与生态位的特殊性。确实，商业采集鼓励梅拉图斯人欣赏雨林生物多样性，尽管它有时也让特定物种因贸易而被过度采伐。这一论证与关于土著知识的刻板印象相悖；一个社群对森林的知识越详细，人们就越假设它与周围世界没有接触。然而，林产品贸易造就了目光敏锐的采集者，他们渴望识别新物种。商业化也确实可能迅速毁掉森林。正如我在第一章所述，东侧森林在20世纪90年代变成了一场任意破坏的狂欢。知识丰富的梅拉图斯采集者与毫无头绪的外来者一道，赶在想象中的终结之前掠夺地景。在这种背景下，很容易看出，同样敏锐的眼睛和耳朵，既能捕捉市场传闻和森林多样性带来的机会，也可能转向加入边疆式破坏，或转向加强长期森林维护。什么解释了这种差异？

In the central mountains, forest collecting has been a feature of subsistence as well as an activity for the market. Collecting is integrated into the possibilities of continuing to live with the forest; it both adds to ordinary living and produces a cash income. In the east-side frontier situation, collecting destroys the possibility of continuing to live in a forested landscape; in the central mountains, collecting makes it possible to continue living with the forest. Collecting for the market does not jeopardize subsistence; it enhances it. Forest collecting in this area takes place in the gap between subsistence and market-oriented economies. Forest products go in and out of market value, but residents continue to appreciate them as landscape features because of their local, subsistence uses. That appreciation allows a quick response to new market conditions. Whether or not this promotes ideal forest conservation policies, it is certainly many times better for the nonhuman residents of the forest than the resource frontier. The fact that there are any forests at all on the island of Borneo today, indeed, attests to the long-term forest-maintenance possibilities in the gap between subsistence and trade.

在中部山区，森林采集一直是生计的一部分，也是面向市场的活动。采集融入继续与森林共居的可能性之中；它既补充日常生活，也带来现金收入。在东侧边疆情境中，采集破坏继续生活在森林地景中的可能性；在中部山区，采集使继续与森林共居成为可能。为市场采集并不危及生计；它增强生计。这一地区的森林采集发生在生计经济与市场导向经济之间的空白中。林产品进出市场价值，但居民因其本地生计用途，继续把它们作为地景特征来珍视。这种珍视使人们能够对新市场状况迅速作出反应。无论这是否促进理想的森林保护政策，对森林中的非人类居民来说，它肯定比资源边疆好上许多倍。事实上，今天婆罗洲岛上还有森林存在，这本身就证明了在生计与贸易之间的空白中，长期维护森林的可能性。

Urban stereotypes guide us to think that the difference between sustainable collecting and frontier destruction is the resilience of “local culture”; yet in fact this difference has everything to do with the relation between forest collectors and downstream traders. Downstream traders buy forest products from Meratus collectors. In some cases, they sell what they have gained further downstream, distributing the products to more specialized buyers. In other cases, they are the specialized buyers, bringing the forest products to their manufacturing or marketing concerns. The most important characteristic of the downstream traders who buy from central mountain Meratus collectors is their willingness to buy small quantities. In contrast, the eastside frontier situation has been stimulated in part by downstream entrepreneurs who only want large quantities, and thus force collectors to organize for scale. The presence of arms, and the armed forces, on the east-side frontier enforces massive extractions. In the central mountains, where soldiers and police rarely venture, it is possible to collect at a slower rate and with more careful methods.

城市刻板印象引导我们以为，可持续采集与边疆破坏之间的差别在于“地方文化”的韧性；然而事实上，这种差别完全取决于森林采集者与下游商人之间的关系。下游商人从梅拉图斯采集者那里购买林产品。在某些情况下，他们把所得进一步向下游出售，把产品分销给更专门的买家。在另一些情况下，他们就是专门买家，把林产品带入自己的制造或营销业务。从中部山区梅拉图斯采集者那里购货的下游商人，最重要的特征是愿意购买小量货物。相比之下，东侧边疆情境部分是由只想要大量货物的下游企业家刺激起来的，他们因此迫使采集者组织起来追求规模。东侧边疆的武器和武装力量，强制进行大规模开采。在中部山区，士兵和警察很少涉足，可以以较慢的速度和较谨慎的方法采集。

Coercion is not irrelevant in the central mountains. Collection has been stimulated by state requirements, ranging from a precolonial gold tax, through the 1930s colonial “coupons” through which Meratus were organized to plant certain amounts of rubber, to the provincial forced rattan deliveries in the 1950s, in which the Banjarmasin furniture industry was stimulated through cheaply obtained materials.

Meratus collectors appreciate connections between downstream traders and the coercive apparatus of the state, which make it difficult for Meratus collectors to gain any bargaining power in selling forest products. Collectors’ disadvantage is enhanced by the cultural differences between collectors and downstream traders, in which downstream traders see themselves as cosmopolitans dealing with a primitive people. Blocked by their cultural distinction, Meratus collectors cannot bypass their downstream traders to negotiate directly with larger manufacturers and merchants; they are forced to accept small sums. At the same time, this cultural difference has stimulated a certain distance, which works to the advantage of collectors: Downstream traders are unfamiliar with—and afraid of—the forest. Downstream traders work with Meratus collectors because they are unable to find forest products by themselves. This ambiguous inequality stabilizes the position of downstream traders as middlemen between collectors and larger merchants and manufacturers. Without the coercive apparatus to press deeper into the forest, these traders are content to gather Meratus collections. It is in this balance that the trade has come to be characterized by exotic products, small quantities, and sporadic and changing market demand.
强制在中部山区并非无关紧要。采集受到国家要求的刺激：从前殖民时期的黄金税，到1930年代殖民“票证”——通过它组织梅拉图斯人种植一定数量的橡胶，再到1950年代省级强制藤条交付——班贾尔马辛家具业靠廉价获得的原料而兴旺。

梅拉图斯采集者清楚下游商人与国家强制机器之间的联系，这使他们在出售林产品时难以获得任何议价能力。采集者与下游商人之间的文化差异加剧了他们的劣势；下游商人把自己看作与原始民族打交道的世界主义者。受文化区隔阻碍，梅拉图斯采集者无法绕过下游商人直接与大制造商和商人谈判；他们被迫接受小笔款项。同时，这种文化差异也制造了一定距离，反而有利于采集者：下游商人不熟悉——而且害怕——森林。下游商人之所以与梅拉图斯采集者合作，是因为他们自己找不到林产品。这种模棱两可的不平等，稳定了下游商人作为采集者与大商人、制造商之间中间人的位置。由于没有深入森林的强制机器，这些商人满足于收集梅拉图斯人的采集物。正是在这种平衡中，贸易形成了异域产品、小量货物、零散多变市场需求的特点。

Meratus collectors respond to the sporadic nature of demand by flooding the market whenever prices are high. They see themselves as powerless to set the terms of the market; they ignore it or respond to it. Given that the market mainly consists of products for which there is a small demand, flooding the market tends to cause a glut; prices drop, and no one collects anymore. If the product’s price stays high, its supply tends to run out, having a similar effect on the collector, although a worse effect on the species being collected. Collectors come to expect these mini-booms and busts. The effect on a particular nonhuman species depends on how it is being collected; some do badly, while others survive. For collectors, both sporadic demand and boom-and-bust cycles stimulate attention to the diversity of forest products, for when one fails, another can be sought. The collector must cultivate an awareness of the varied opportunities of the forest.

梅拉图斯采集者应对需求零散性的方式，是价格高时就向市场大量供货。他们觉得自己无力设定市场条件；他们忽视它或回应它。鉴于市场主要由需求量小的产品构成，大量供货往往造成市场过剩；价格下跌，就没人再采集。如果产品价格居高不下，其供应往往会耗尽，对采集者产生类似效果，尽管对被采集的物种更糟。采集者逐渐预期这些小型繁荣与萧条。对特定非人类物种的影响取决于采集方式；有些损失惨重，另一些则存活下来。对采集者来说，零散需求与繁荣—萧条周期都促使他们关注林产品的多样性，因为一种失败了，还可以寻找另一种。采集者必须培养对森林各种机会的敏锐意识。

The only practical way to make this work in the central mountains is to integrate commercial collecting into ordinary life maintainence, that is, subsistence. No one tries to survive by commercial collection alone, and while the income gained from commercial collection is important, used for clothing, tools, bridewealth, luxuries, and government exactments, no cash is required for food, shelter, and everyday sociability, which are gained from local supplies in fields and forests. Commercial collecting must fit into the schedule of subsistence labor. Men are only able to wander the forest when the work of swidden agriculture is being covered by women, as it is during the seasons for weeding, guarding the rice, and harvesting. During these seasons, as well as the period between the rice harvest and the preparation of new fields, men are free to combine commercial and subsistence collecting, bringing home wild pigs, fruit, bamboo shoots, firewood, and resin for torches, as well as products for the market.

在中部山区，让这一切可行的唯一实际方式，是把商业采集融入日常生活维持，也就是生计。没有人试图仅靠商业采集生存；商业采集所得的收入固然重要，用于购买衣物、工具、聘礼、奢侈品和应付政府征收，但食物、住所和日常社交不需要现金，这些来自田地和森林的本地供应。商业采集必须配合生计劳动的日程。只有在刀耕火种农业的劳动由女性承担时——如在除草、看护稻谷和收获季节——男性才能漫游森林。在这些季节，以及稻谷收获与新田准备之间的时期，男性可以自由地把商业采集与生计采集结合起来，带回家野猪、水果、竹笋、柴火和火把用树脂，以及供市场销售的产品。

Collecting, whether for subsistence or commercial purposes, requires an intimate familiarity with particular areas of forest. A few things are best found by roaming around large unfamiliar areas, but most collecting is facilitated by knowing the terrain (Is the plant specific to montane areas?), the ecological community (Is this a riverside plant? A plant that will grow in young secondary forest?), and the very specific natural history of particular sites, which have come to be characterized by some species and not others. Although models of optimal foraging rarely take this into account, any reader who has ever tried to locate a wildflower or even an animal site probably knows that it really helps to know the particular places, and not just the ecologically appropriate kinds of places, that plant or animal has been seen before; that’s the place to find it again. Meratus collectors know particular sections of the forest very well, and these are the starting points for their collections. They learn these sections because they go there all the time: to hunt, to look for fruit and honey, to find old cultivates in the regrowing forest that once was their swidden or that of their great aunts, and to find saleable forest products. They learn these forest places in activities that span the gap between subsistence and trade.

采集，无论为了生计还是商业目的，都需要对特定森林区域有亲密熟悉。少数东西最好在大片不熟悉区域漫游时找到，但大多数采集得益于了解地形（这种植物只长在山地吗？）、生态群落（这是河岸植物吗？一种会在年轻次生林生长的植物吗？），以及特定地点的非常具体的自然史——这些地点已以某些物种而非其他物种为特征。虽然最优觅食模型很少考虑这一点，但任何曾试图寻找野花甚至某处动物栖息地的读者大概都知道，真正有帮助的是知道这种植物或动物以前被见过的那些特定地点，而不只是生态上合适的地点；那才是再次找到它的地方。梅拉图斯采集者非常了解森林的特定地段，这些是他们采集的起点。他们了解这些地段，是因为他们总去那里：打猎，寻找水果和蜂蜜，在再生林中寻找旧栽培植物——那里曾是他们的刀耕火种田，或他们祖辈姐妹的田——以及寻找可销售的林产品。他们在横跨生计与贸易之空白的活动中了解这些森林地点。

These familiar territories are not exactly private property, although they come to be associated with particular groups of people. The familiar territories of individuals interpenetrate and overlap; they are not exclusive or bounded. Yet these territories also limit and organize forest management, as well as collection. Familiar territories inspire a neighborly respect that keeps people from straying too far, too long, into forest territories associated with another group of people. (There one may stumble on to a disguised but deadly spring trap, set for pigs or deer. In familiar forest, one knows where the traps are.) Familiar territories inspire an alertness in one’s own “home” spaces: Which tree species are flowering? Which holes in the creek contain edible minnows? Which animal tracks have been sighted? Which honey trees are being smothered by strangling vines? This alertness is a form of attention to biological diversity, not only as a list of species, but also as growth habits, population dynamics, species associations, and ecological histories. Meratus were able to tell me so much about the forest because of this kind of alertness, grown over time in familiar territories. From it, collectors have the ability to choose products for the market, to supply local needs, and to develop a sense of the diverse relations linking humans with forest animals and plants.

这些熟悉的领地并不完全是私有财产，尽管它们会与特定人群联系在一起。个人的熟悉领地相互渗透、重叠；它们并不排他，也没有边界。然而这些领地也限制并组织森林管理与采集。熟悉的领地激发一种邻里式的尊重，使人们不会过于深入、过于长久地进入与另一群人相关的森林领地。（在那里，人们可能撞上为野猪或鹿设置、伪装却致命的弹簧陷阱。在熟悉的森林里，人们知道陷阱在哪里。）熟悉的领地激发人对自己的“家”空间保持警觉：哪些树种正在开花？溪流哪些深潭里有可食的小鱼？发现过哪些动物足迹？哪些蜜树正被绞杀藤覆盖？这种警觉是对生物多样性的一种关注，不仅是物种清单，还包括生长习性、种群动态、物种关联和生态史。梅拉图斯人能够告诉我这么多关于森林的事，正是因为这种警觉在熟悉的领地中随时间生长起来。由此，采集者有能力为市场选择产品、供应本地需求，并发展出对人类与森林动植物之间多样关系的感知。

Let me turn to one example: rattans. Rattans are spiny, vinelike climbing palms. Their often-barbed thorns help them catch hold of surrounding vegetation, as they rise through the forest; they also tear the flesh of animals who come too near, including hikers unfortunate enough to brush against their ever-present extensions across the trail. The stems of rattans are long, flexible, and strong; people around the world have thought of many uses for them, particularly in furniture making, mats, and basketry. In the 1980s, and into the 1990s until the local supply ran out, rattan was the most important product of central mountain trade. One species dominated above all others: huyi saga (Calamus caesius). In east-side areas where rattan could be rafted out, huyi saga was often sold in long looped bundles, called galung “coils.” In the central mountains, however, transportation of such heavy bundles was too difficult, and rattan was generally prepared by cutting it carefully into neat strips. Coarse strips (lampit) were sold to the mat-making industry; fine, delicately worked strips were sold for ties, baskets, and the woven-cane furniture industry.

让我举一个例子：棕榈藤。棕榈藤是带刺、呈藤状攀缘的棕榈。它们常常带倒钩的刺帮助它们攀附周围植被，在森林中向上生长；这些刺也会撕裂靠得太近的动物皮肉，包括不幸擦到它们横在小径上、无处不在的延伸茎的徒步者。藤茎长、柔韧而结实；世界各地的人想出了许多用途，尤其是家具制造、席子和篮筐编织。20世纪80年代直至90年代本地供应耗尽，藤是中部山区贸易最重要的产品。一个物种占据压倒性主导地位：huyi saga（Calamus caesius）。在东侧地区，藤可以顺水筏运，huyi saga 常以长环状捆出售，称为 galung，“盘卷”。然而在中部山区，运输如此沉重的捆扎太困难，藤一般被仔细切成整齐的条状。粗条（lampit）卖给制席业；精细加工的细条则卖给绑扎、篮筐和藤编家具业。

Huyi saga is, at least ideally, a renewable resource. If the collector leaves a length of stem at the base of the plant, the rattan will regenerate. Furthermore, it has become a cultivated crop, planted in swiddens to be harvested beginning six to eight years later. Even without planting, there is a reasonable chance that huyi saga will develop in the swidden regrowth. Secondary forest, with its stronger light, is a beneficial environment for the growth of many rattans, including huyi saga. Huyi saga fruits annually and abundantly with edible, sour fruits that are widely spread by wild animals. In the central mountains, swidden-making and rattan growth do reasonably well together.

至少在理想情况下，huyi saga 是可再生资源。如果采集者在植株基部留下一段茎，藤就会再生。此外，它已成为一种栽培作物，种在刀耕火种田里，六到八年后开始收获。即使不栽种，huyi saga 也有相当机会在刀耕火种后的再生林中生长。次生林光线较强，是许多藤类——包括 huyi saga——生长的有利环境。huyi saga 每年大量结果，果实可食且酸，被野生动物广泛传播。在中部山区，刀耕火种与藤的生长配合得相当好。

By the early 1990s, however, huyi saga had become scarce in the Meratus Mountains. How had this happened? Indonesian national policy promoted rattan exports in the 1980s and encouraged rattan buyers, who formed contacts with a greater variety of transnational manufacturers. Prices were high; a lot of rattan was wanted. Policy excitement about rattan pushed groups of adventurers from the plains into the mountains to cut rattan themselves. These adventurers cut planted and protected rattan as well as rattan in mature forest; nor did they have any motivation to cut it in such a way as to allow regeneration. Without any protection for the rattan they had planted and encouraged, Meratus began to cut their own rattan before someone else could steal it. The competition to sell rattan grew to a high pitch; suddenly, there was no more saleable huyi saga.

然而到20世纪90年代初，huyi saga 在梅拉图斯山脉已经稀少。这是怎么发生的？印尼国家政策在20世纪80年代推动藤出口，鼓励藤商与更多种类的跨国制造商建立联系。价格很高；需要大量藤条。政策引发的藤业热潮，促使一群群平原冒险者进山自己砍藤。这些冒险者砍伐栽种和受保护的藤，也砍伐成熟森林中的藤；他们也没有任何动机以利于再生的方式砍伐。梅拉图斯人栽种和培育的藤得不到任何保护，于是他们开始赶在别人偷走之前砍自己的藤。出售藤的竞争达到白热化；突然间，再也没有可供出售的 huyi saga 了。
Luckily, huyi saga is only one of many kinds of useful rattan that prosper in the central mountains.

Before the 1950s, many kinds of rattan were sold on the market. The focus on huyi saga was artificially created by government working together with industry; the forced rattan deliveries of the 1950s not only stimulated provincial industry but also advised Meratus of new conditions of trade. When huyi saga ran out in the 1990s, there was some optimism among Meratus collectors that traders would pick up on other species. Handicrafts, such as baskets, made from other rattans were still saleable. Moreover, the diversity of rattans meant that the scarcity of huyi saga was not felt in relation to subsistence uses of rattan, and there was no need to cut it as it regenerated in old fields and forest.
幸运的是，huyi saga 只是中部山区繁茂生长的许多有用藤类之一。

20世纪50年代以前，许多种藤在市场上出售。对 huyi saga 的集中关注，是政府与产业合作人为制造出来的；1950年代的强制藤条交付不仅刺激了省级产业，也让梅拉图斯人得知新的贸易条件。当 huyi saga 在20世纪90年代耗尽时，梅拉图斯采集者中间存在一些乐观情绪，认为商人会转向其他物种。用其他藤编织的篮筐等手工艺品仍有销路。此外，藤的多样性意味着 huyi saga 的稀缺并未影响藤的生计用途，也就不必在它于旧田和森林中再生时砍伐它。

Huyi saga is not the only commercial species. Manau is a thick cane rattan whose fruits and buds are favored foods and whose cane is used for the rims of large baskets. The canes, brought to market as long, thick sticks, are called walatung. Bent into chairs and sofa legs, they are another staple of the furniture industry. In the 1980s, the market for manau soared. Collecting boomed in the Meratus Mountains. As with huyi saga, it is possible to cut manau in such a way that the rattan regenerates, but when collecting goes wild, many collectors ignore this. One odd circumstance helped save local populations. The stem of another large cane rattan, minung, looks very much like manau. It is easy for Meratus collectors to tell the difference, but it is not easy for the traders who buy from them to differentiate the species. Minung has a brittle stem; it is not suitable for furniture making. According to my Meratus friends, it can “break the machine.” Meratus collectors often substituted minung for manau in selling cane. When this happened, the market died for a while, whether because the provincial machines were out of order or because the traders had lost faith in Meratus collectors. This lent a particularly sporadic tenor to the manau market.

huyi saga 不是唯一的商业物种。马瑙藤（manau）是一种粗藤，其果实和芽是受人喜爱的食物，其藤用于大篮筐的边框。作为又长又粗的藤条带到市场的，称为 walatung。弯成椅子和沙发腿，它们是家具业的另一种主要原料。20世纪80年代，马瑙藤市场飙升。梅拉图斯山脉的采集繁荣起来。与 huyi saga 一样，可以以利于再生的方式砍马瑙藤，但当采集失控时，许多采集者忽视这一点。一个奇怪的情况帮助拯救了当地种群。另一种大藤 minung 的茎看起来很像 manau。梅拉图斯采集者很容易分辨，但从他们那里购货的商人却不容易区分物种。Minung 的茎易脆，不适合做家具。据我的梅拉图斯朋友说，它能“弄坏机器”。梅拉图斯采集者在出售藤条时常用 minung 顶替 manau。这种情况发生时，市场会死一段时间，或因为省内工厂的机器出了故障，或因为商人不再信任梅拉图斯采集者。这使 manau 的市场需求格外时断时续。

Rattans, in their variety, move in and out of “resource” status in the Meratus Mountains. Relations between collectors and downstream traders are an essential ingredient in making a rattan a commercial resource. This resource status, in turn, can provoke a number of different responses from Meratus collectors. Wild overcutting is one response. Overcutting depletes the product, wiping out its resource status at least for awhile. Domestication is another response. Cultivated plants can form a steadier supply for both traders and planters, but traders are tempted, too, to send their own armed men to get these more easily locatable cultivates as long as local claims are unprotected by the state. A third response is the collectors’ attempt to substitute related species. Because collectors tend to know species variety better than traders do, this last response, in particular, keeps the traders wary and puzzled, dependent on their collectors. When coercive interventions become possible, as for example, with the entry of the army into the trade, they bypass local collectors altogether to guarantee the homogeneity of the resource and interlopers’ free rights over it. But thus, too, they are likely to wipe out the resource entirely.

藤类以其多样性在梅拉图斯山脉进出“资源”地位。采集者与下游商人之间的关系，是使某种藤成为商业资源的关键成分。这种资源地位又会引发梅拉图斯采集者的若干不同反应。失控的过度砍伐是一种反应。过度砍伐耗尽产品，至少暂时抹去其资源地位。驯化是另一种反应。栽培植物能为商人和种植者提供更稳定的供应，但只要地方认领得不到国家保护，商人也想派自己的武装人员去获取这些更容易找到的栽培物。第三种反应是采集者尝试用近缘物种替代原先收购的物种。由于采集者往往比商人更了解物种多样性，这最后一种反应尤其让商人保持警惕和困惑，依赖他们的采集者。当强制干预成为可能，例如军队进入贸易，商人便会完全绕过当地采集者，以保证资源的同质性以及闯入者对其自由支配的权利。但这样一来，他们也很可能把资源彻底耗尽。

It is within these tensions and instabilities that Meratus collectors scan the forests for useable and saleable products. The knowledge they bring to forest collection is not a closed, traditional knowledge but rather one that is constantly augmented by their sense of their relationship with downstream traders, of changing market demands, and of the conditions under which they can claim and sell their products. While this knowledge includes an appreciation for biodiversity, it may or may not nurture and protect nonhuman species. Yet the one thing that is utterly clear is that central mountain collectors are doing a whole lot better than the development experts and agents who surround them on almost every side.

正是在这些紧张与不稳定之中，梅拉图斯采集者搜寻森林，寻找可用和可销售的产品。他们带到森林采集中的知识，不是封闭的传统知识，而是一种不断被他们对与下游商人关系的感知、对变化的市场需求的感知，以及对能够认领和出售产品条件的感知所增补的知识。这种知识包含对生物多样性的欣赏，但它可能滋养并保护非人类物种，也可能不会。然而完全清楚的一点是，中部山区的采集者比几乎从四面八方包围他们的发展专家和代理人做得好得多。
Inside the Gap between Farm and Forest
在农田与森林之间的空白内部

In the central mountains, swidden farms are constantly becoming forest. In 1986, when I visited the swidden field next to which I lived in 1981, I found it a dark, shady place, thick with wild gingers rising up above my head: patitih, patikang, patikala, pitukun. Each of these members of the ginger family, Zingiberaceae, is a giant herb with flowers reminiscent of colorful sea creatures, and tall, glossy leaves that may reach up ten or twelve feet. I saw no trace of the grasses and weedy annuals with wind-borne seeds that are the first pioneers of open places; the shade had long ago discouraged them. Eventually, the gingers would die back too. There was already a variety of young secondary forest trees, such as the gangly ground-figs, dandali, with their juicy red fruits peeking from the ground. On one margin, people had maintained a small clearing next to the trail, and a few papaya trees from the old swidden still stood. Most of the other light-demanding swidden plants were gone, at least to my eyes, replaced by a young forest. Meratus say that after five years, the trees in jurungan “secondary forest regrowth” reach a diameter as big as one’s arm. In ten years, they reach the size of a person’s leg. When I visited the same place in 1994, the trees were substantial, and, despite my clear memories of bends and rocks in the stream that runs along one border, I had trouble picking the area out from surrounding forest.

在中部山区，刀耕火种农田不断变成森林。1986年，我重访一块刀耕火种田，1981年我就住在它旁边，发现它已成幽暗阴凉之处，长满高过我头顶的野姜：patitih、patikang、patikala、pitukun。这些姜科（Zingiberaceae）成员每一株都是巨型草本，花朵令人想起色彩斑斓的海洋生物，高挑而有光泽的叶子可伸展至十到十二英尺高处。我看不到开阔地最早的拓殖者——那些种子随风传播的禾草和杂草性一年生植物——的任何痕迹；浓荫早已使它们退却。最终，野姜也会枯退。这里已经有多种年轻的次生林树木，比如细长的地榕 dandali，多汁的红色果实从地面探出。在一侧边缘，人们在步道旁保留了一小块空地，旧田里还有几棵木瓜树。其他大多数喜光的刀耕火种植物，至少在我看来已经消失，被一片年轻森林取代。梅拉图斯人说，五年后，jurungan（次生林再生）中的树木会长到手臂那么粗。十年后，它们会长到人腿那么粗。1994年我重访同一地点时，树木已经很大；尽管我清楚记得沿一侧边界流淌的溪流有转弯和岩石，我还是很难从周围森林中辨出那块地。

Regrowing secondary forests, like this one, have never garnered sympathetic attention among either scholars or policy makers; they are not a popular place among either developers or conservationists. Developers see secondary forest as abandoned agriculture or degraded timber land; it is a place of waste, where the human mastery of nature has been neglected. Conservationists see it as weedy brush, full of easily spreading species that contrast in their dense homogeneity with the complex but open architecture of the mature rainforest. Yet one might also see secondary forest as a site of possibility for both livelihood and species protection. For those who have become familiar with its wild species and enrich it with their plantings, the secondary forest is not only a place of useful products but also a place dedicated to the regrowing future. Under the best conditions, secondary forest gains architectural complexity and diversity: In fifty years, pioneer species are being shaded out by mature forest species coming into their own; and although it may take centuries to gain certain kinds of complexity, within a hundred years the forest has a formidable species diversity. Now it takes a particular kind of landscape dynamic to nurture fifty- and one hundred-year old forest regrowth. We might want to know something about it. As long as both developers and conservationists divide up the land into zones of intensive agriculture and zones of pristine nature, no such patches of regrowth and possibility will be acknowledged. The central Meratus Mountains will continue to be invisible, or worse yet, criminal.

像这样的再生次生林，从未得到学者或政策制定者的同情关注；它们既不受开发商也不受保护主义者欢迎。开发商把次生林看作被弃置的农业或被退化的林地；那是一片浪费之地，人类对自然的掌控在那里遭到忽视。保护主义者把它看作杂草灌木，满是容易蔓延的物种，其稠密同质性恰与成熟雨林复杂而开阔的建筑结构形成对比。然而，人们也可以把次生林视为兼具生计与物种保护可能性的场所。对于那些熟悉其野生物种、并用栽种丰富它的人来说，次生林不仅是有用产品之地，也是一片献给再生未来的地方。在最佳条件下，次生林会获得建筑复杂性与多样性：五十年内，先锋物种会被成熟森林物种遮死，后者逐渐占据优势；虽然获得某些复杂性可能需要数百年，但一百年内，森林已拥有可观的物种多样性。培育五十年和一百年的森林再生，需要一种特殊的地景动态。我们也许想对它有所了解。只要开发商和保护主义者都把土地划分为集约农业区和原始自然区，这些再生与可能性的斑块就不会得到承认。中梅拉图斯山脉将继续不可见，或更糟，被认定为违法之地。

How might we learn something from the landscape of regrowing forest? Again, it makes sense to ask how its Meratus inhabitants know it. Here the key is that secondary forest is always a social place; to know it is to know the history of its flora and fauna in relation to socially situated human biographies. Secondary forest is always familiar forest for some group of people; people are attached to it because they once made a swidden there and because they have continued to maintain their relationship with the regrowing forest vegetation. Long-term biographical connections between people and forest regrowth are the basis of Meratus forest knowledge and management practices.
我们如何能从再生森林的地景中学到东西？在此，询问梅拉图斯居民如何认识它同样有道理。关键在于，次生林始终是一个社会性场所；认识它，就是认识其动植物群系与社会处境化的人生传记相关的历史。对某些人群来说，次生林始终是熟悉的森林；人们依恋它，因为他们曾在那里开垦过刀耕火种田，并一直与再生的森林植被维持关系。人与森林再生之间长期的传记性联系，是梅拉图斯森林知识与管理实践的基础。

The process of forming that dense knowledge of vegetation that forges connections between people and places begins in the swidden field itself. As I have said, some large trees, such as fruit and honey trees, are saved in the process of swidden-making. These will continue to form elements of the new forest that grows on the site. Some other trees, too, do not die in the process of swidden-making. Although woody growth is cut and burned in swidden-making, burning is only rarely intense and thorough in the Meratus Mountains. Some trees sprout from their stumps and eventually resume their status in the forest. Other woody plants also resprout from their roots if they are not killed in the weeding process. Meratus weeders cut weeds back but do not uproot them; this discourages soft-stemmed herbs more than woody plants. Some shrubs, ferns, and bamboos grow back. These regrowing elements of the old forest are the most basic resources of the regrowing forest.

形成这种关于植被的细密知识——它缔结人与地方之间的联系——的过程，始于刀耕火种田本身。如我所说，一些大树，例如果树和蜜树，会在开垦过程中被保留。它们将继续构成生长于该地的新森林的元素。另一些树也不会在开垦过程中死亡。虽然木本植被在刀耕火种中被砍倒并焚烧，但在梅拉图斯山脉，焚烧很少强烈而彻底。有些树从树桩上发芽，最终恢复其在森林中的地位。其他木本植物如果在除草过程中没有被杀死，也会从根部重新发芽。梅拉图斯人除草时把杂草割回，但不连根拔起；这更多抑制软茎草本，而非木本植物。一些灌木、蕨类和竹子重新生长。这些旧森林的再生元素，是再生森林最基本的资源。

Weeders get to know, too, the new plants of the swidden, whether they are unwelcome pests or valued wild vegetables and medicinal herbs. Many wild plants are encouraged in the swidden, such as the sweet-bitter wild cucumber, hantikup, known only as a swidden intruder. (Hantikup disappears in the shady regrowing forest; but if a swidden is cleared on this site again, it predictably reappears from seeds still in the soil. A history of hantikup is one reason, people said, to reuse a forest regrowth site for a swidden.) Women and children tend to know the most about the weeds, grasses, and herbs of young regrowth. Women learn them from weeding and children from playing in and around the fields. They remember these weeds and herbs as the swidden grows into forest.

除草者也逐渐认识刀耕火种田里的新植物，无论它们是不受欢迎的杂草，还是珍贵的野生蔬菜和草药。许多野生植物在刀耕火种田里受到促进，比如甜苦兼具的野黄瓜汉蒂库普（hantikup），人们只知道它是刀耕火种田的入侵者。（汉蒂库普会在阴暗的再生林中消失；但如果再次在该地点开垦刀耕火种田，它可预见地会从仍在土壤中的种子重新出现。人们说，此地曾长过汉蒂库普，是重新利用次生林地点开垦刀耕火种田的一个理由。）女性和儿童往往最了解年轻再生林中的杂草、禾草和草本。女性通过除草学习它们，儿童则在田里和田边玩耍时学习。当刀耕火种田长成森林时，他们仍记得这些杂草和草本。

For the first few years after the swidden’s last rice crop, there is still much to harvest in the old swidden: banana trees produce new suckers; papayas fruit; taro and other aroids grow in the shade; herbs planted in the swidden flourish in the forest cover. After five or six years, there will not be much left of these short-term crops, but some of the fruit trees people planted will be bearing. In the process of keeping track of such crops, women and children also acquaint themselves with the regrowing secondary forest, looking for its own distinctive vegetation. Many of the most popular snack foods for women and children are found in young secondary forest. The sour fruit of wild gingers or the sweet berries of mampap vines are always a welcome find. Young secondary forest is also the favored site for collecting herbs for medicines and poultices, for beauty aids such as hair conditioners, for ritual equipment, for household tools, and for children’s toys. Each time a person comes to collect a particular species, she notices the other species that have taken their places beside it in the regrowth. In this close attention to species distribution, over repeated visits, the familiarity of the site and its vegetation is continually enhanced.

刀耕火种田最后一季稻谷收获后的最初几年，旧田里仍有很多可收获的东西：香蕉树长出新吸芽；木瓜结果；芋头和其他天南星科植物在阴凉处生长；种在田里的草本植物在森林覆盖下繁茂。五六年之后，这些短期作物剩不下多少，但人们栽种的一些果树将开始结果。在照看这些作物的过程中，女性和儿童也熟悉再生的次生林，寻找它特有的植被。女性和儿童最喜爱的许多零食，都来自年轻的次生林。野姜的酸果或马姆帕普（mampap）藤的甜浆果，总是受欢迎的发现。年轻次生林也是采集草本植物以制作药物与敷剂、美容用品（如护发用品）、仪式用品、家用工具及儿童玩具的首选地点。每次一个人来采集某个特定物种，她都会注意到再生林中在旁边占据位置的其他物种。在对物种分布的密切关注中，经过反复造访，对地点及其植被的熟悉不断增强。

The light gap of swidden regrowth encourages not only the quick-growing herbs and soft-wooded trees that will soon-enough be shaded out by other species but also a variety of plants that have a reasonably long-lasting presence in the regrowing forest. Familiarity with and use of these long-living “weeds” is one source of protected diversity in the forest. Bamboos, for example, are encouraged by swidden-making—and much valued by Meratus for their many uses. Bamboos grow in exuberant variety in the central Meratus Mountains. The most common, paring, is used for basket-making when the plant is young, for roof tiles when mature, and for firewood when old. The much sturdier batung makes house poles, rafts, and the aqueducts that carry clean spring water to convenient water-collecting sites. Batung is planted in swiddens in some west-side Meratus areas where it can be rafted into lowland markets as a cash crop; its stability as a forest plant also makes it an important marker of swidden-based forest claims in areas where immigrants may not otherwise recognize land rights. Batung, planted in swiddens made in areas in which grasses such as hilalang (Imperata cylindrica) threaten forest succession, maintains the shady ecology that allows forest plants to dominate the regrowing swidden patch. In the central mountains, however, forest successions are not threatened, and batung is rarely planted. However, like other bamboos, it does not die when cut back in swiddens; it grows back with vigor.

刀耕火种再生的光隙，不仅促进那些很快会被其他物种遮死的速生草本和木质较软的树，也促进多种在再生林中存在相当久的植物。对这些长寿“杂草”的熟悉与利用，是森林中受保护多样性的一种来源。例如，竹子因刀耕火种而受到促进——也因其多种用途深受梅拉图斯人重视。竹子在中梅拉图斯山脉生长得极为丰富多样。最常见的帕林竹（paring），幼时用于编篮，成熟时用于屋顶瓦片，老时作柴火。更为粗壮的巴通竹（batung）用于制作房柱、竹筏，以及把清洁泉水引到方便取水处的引水槽。在西侧一些梅拉图斯地区，巴通竹种在刀耕火种田里，可顺水筏运到低地市场作为经济作物；它作为森林植物的稳定性，也使其成为刀耕火种森林认领的重要标志，在移民可能不承认土地权利的地区尤其如此。在 hilalang（Imperata cylindrica，白茅）等禾草威胁森林演替的地区，种在刀耕火种田里的巴通竹维持阴凉生态，让森林植物能在再生斑块中占优势。然而在中部山区，森林演替不受威胁，巴通竹很少被栽种。不过，像其他竹子一样，它在刀耕火种田里被砍伐后不会死亡；它会旺盛地重新生长。

The sweetest, freshest tasting bamboo shoots are from one batung species, batung manis. Other batung, such as batung raya, have huge stems, which can be used as large containers. Most ordinary water and food containers are made from a more delicate species group, buluh. Buluh has thin walls, which can be unrolled to make temporary floors and walls for houses. Buluh kuning, a buluh with yellow culms, is in demand for certain rituals. The thin-stemmed tirik is used for fine weaving and small-bored flutes. Meratus use bamboo for many purposes, and they need to know where many kinds can be found. They return to bamboo stands in familiar secondary forest to harvest the culms they need. The persistence of bamboo in secondary forest draws them, sponsoring the knowledge and long-term relationships between people and plants through which familiar forest is made.

最甜、最新鲜的竹笋来自一种巴通竹，batung manis。其他巴通竹，如 batung raya，茎很大，可用作大型容器。大多数普通的水容器和食物容器，用一种更精细的竹类群 buluh 制作。Buluh 壁薄，可以展开，做成临时地板和房屋墙壁。Buluh kuning 是一种秆呈黄色的 buluh，在某些仪式中很受欢迎。细茎的 tirik 用于精细编织和细管笛。梅拉图斯人把竹子用于许多目的，他们需要知道哪里能找到许多种类。他们回到熟悉次生林中的竹林，采伐所需的竹秆。竹子在次生林中的持续存在吸引着他们，促成了人与植物之间的知识和长期关系，熟悉的森林由此形成。

Palms are also encouraged in the regrowing forest. Some palms are planted: coconut palms, which may die when a bear eats the (really delicious) growing bud; areca palms, which supply valued betel quids; marsh-loving rumbiah sago palms, whose starchy pith yields an important hunger food; and, of course, rattans. Other palms thrive in the swidden’s light gap: the thatch palm haping; the minor sago palms risi and mangkung. A number of palms do not die in swidden-making; bangkala, for example, grows new stems when cut down, and after five years these can be harvested for the tasty palm-hearts. Some palms, too, run the full range of forms of encouragement. Hanau sugar palms may be saved, planted, encouraged, or merely tolerated in swiddens. (Sugar is made by bruising and cutting the male inflorescence, collecting the sweet syrup that emerges, and boiling it down until it is close to crystallization.) The importance of palm diversity for Meratus draws them to both learn about and enrich the secondary forest.

棕榈也在再生林中受到促进。有些棕榈是栽种的：椰子树，可能因熊吃掉（非常美味的）生长中的芽而死亡；槟榔树，提供珍贵的槟榔嚼块；喜沼泽的伦比亚（rumbiah）西米棕榈，其淀粉质髓部产出重要的充饥食物；当然还有藤。其他棕榈在刀耕火种田的光隙中繁茂：用作屋顶覆盖材料的棕榈 haping；次要西米棕榈 risi 和 mangkung。一些棕榈不会在刀耕火种中死亡；例如 bangkala 被砍倒后会长出新茎，五年后可采其美味的棕榈心。有些棕榈也涵盖各种促进形式。哈瑙糖棕（hanau）可能在刀耕火种田中被保留、栽种、促进，或仅仅被容忍。（制糖的方法是碾伤并切开雄花序，收集流出的甜汁，煮到接近结晶。）棕榈多样性对梅拉图斯人的重要性，吸引他们既学习也丰富次生林。

Secondary forest becomes familiar forest through attention applied over many years. Secondary forest forms the most basic collecting areas for the people who know it, from which they branch out to find products that grow in old-growth forest or more specialized forest niches. Hiking with Meratus friends through familiar forest, we paused and meandered continually to check the status of fruit trees and taste locally abundant snacks. In contrast, walking through forest associated with a group with whom my friends did not have close relationships, we moved along the trail at a businesslike pace, only rarely stopping to drink or rest. The relationship between social groups and forest patches structures forest management and use. When Meratus discuss their location in the forest, they talk not only of the history of vegetation in that place but also of the social connections that tie those plants to particular people. The forest, whether young or old, is never a homogeneous “wild” place; it is a finely differentiated set of simultaneously social and natural locations.

次生林通过多年投入的关注，变成熟悉的森林。对认识它的人来说，次生林构成最基本的采集区；他们从那里向外扩展，寻找生长在老龄林或更专门森林生态位中的产品。与梅拉图斯朋友在熟悉的森林中徒步时，我们不断停下、迂回，查看果树的状况，品尝当地丰富的零食。相比之下，走进与我朋友没有密切关系的人群相关的森林时，我们以公事公办的步伐沿小径行进，很少停下来喝水或休息。社会群体与森林斑块之间的关系，构成了森林管理与使用的结构。梅拉图斯人讨论自己在森林中的位置时，不仅谈该地植被的历史，也谈把那些植物与特定人群联系起来的纽带。森林，无论年轻还是古老，从来不是同质的“荒野”之地；它是一组精细区分的、同时是社会性和自然性的地点。

Outsiders who come into the mountains rarely see this. Most of us are trained to see nothing but a chaotic mass of green. As one of my friends in the United States put it, “Walking in the forest is boring. It’s not like the streets of a city, full of shops and people; there’s nothing to see.” For Meratus, there is a lot to see. Yet even forest experts have immersed themselves in ways of seeing that dull their eyes to the “city streets” of enriched secondary forest. Most often, very young regrowth, such as the belukar “brush” of Indonesian national land use mapping, is the model for secondary forest. It is imagined as choking with weeds and grasses, a site only of the abandonment of agriculture. The varied circumstances of forest regeneration are lumped together to form an image of messy deterioration.

进山的外来者很少看到这一点。我们大多数人受的训练是只看见一团混乱的绿色。正如我在美国的一位朋友所说：“在森林里走路很无聊。不像城市街道，满是商店和人；这里没什么可看的。”对梅拉图斯人来说，可看的东西很多。然而即使森林专家，也浸淫在某种观看方式中，使他们对丰富次生林的“城市街道”视而不见。最常见的是，印尼国家土地利用制图中的 belukar“灌木丛”这类非常年轻的再生林，成为次生林的模型。它被想象为杂草与禾草蔓生，只是农业被弃置的地点。森林再生的各种不同情况被混为一谈，形成一幅杂乱退化的图像。

Regrowth can be inadequate. The timber operations I saw on the east side of the mountains in the 1980s left landscapes in which one single plant quickly came to dominate: a vine Meratus call balaran. These places were biologically monotonous and unusable for either shifting cultivation or forest product collecting. Without more roots holding the soil, the first severe rains caused massive erosion. The category “secondary regrowth” does not in itself differentiate between this situation and what I saw in the central mountains, where small fields surrounded by forest were reseeded with diverse forest species. Within this confusion, the landscape is misread, to everyone’s detriment: Socially enriched forest is classified as old-growth production forest, to be contracted to loggers, and thus destroyed; or else it is classified as wasteland, to be contracted to plantation development, and thus destroyed.

再生也可能不足。20世纪80年代我在山脉东侧看到的木材作业，留下了单一植物迅速占据主导的地景：一种梅拉图斯人称为巴拉兰（balaran）的藤。这些地方在生物上单调，既不能用于游耕，也不能用于林产品采集。没有更多根系固定土壤，最初几场暴雨就造成大规模侵蚀。“次生再生”这一范畴本身并不能区分这种情况与我在中部山区看到的景象：在中部山区，被森林环绕的小片田地会重新播下多样的森林物种。在这种混淆中，地景被误读，人人受损：经社会实践培育而丰富起来的森林被归类为老龄生产林，承包给伐木者，因而被毁；或者被归类为荒地，承包给种植园开发，因而被毁。

Why is regrowing forest so persistently difficult for experts and planners to see? On one level, a widespread if misleading “common sense” is to blame: Experts and planners are most likely to recognize only the difference between “fields” and “forests” with no connection between them. They are used to fields in permanent cultivation, fields that are “obviously” sources of human livelihood. Whether they see forests as sources of commercial timber or genetic reserves, they are likely to focus only on the completed mosaic of trees, not the process of landscape formation over time. From this snapshot perspective, the difference between a neatly cultivated field and a wild forest is visually sharp. Everything between is matter out of place.

为什么再生森林如此长期地难以被专家和规划者看见？在某个层面上，可以归咎于一种广泛却误导性的“常识”：专家和规划者最可能只承认“田地”与“森林”的差异，而不承认两者之间的联系。他们习惯于永久耕作的田地，那种“显然”是人类生计来源的田地。无论他们把森林视为商业木材来源还是基因库，都可能只关注树木已完成的拼图，而不关注随时间形成的地景过程。从这种快照视角看，整齐栽培的田地与野生森林之间的差异在视觉上十分鲜明。两者之间的一切都是位置不当之物。

This common-sense perspective is common in Indonesia, as it is around the world. Walking through a Meratus rubber orchard (admittedly one growing amidst varied trees), one planner asked me, “How do you like this Indonesian jungle?” as if he were perfectly blind except to random greenness. This kind of blindness would still not mean much for the administration of this area if it were not inscribed into development policy. Development has organized the national exploitation of natural resources. Between the late 1960s and the late 1990s, development directed this exploitation as if the areas in which natural resources were found were, by definition, uninhabited. Development divided the country into dichotomous zones: zones of population and zones of natural resource exploitation. In zones of population, development managed communities. In zones of natural resource exploitation, people were irrelevant. The goal of development was to get out the resources.

这种常识视角在印尼很常见，正如在世界各地一样。走过梅拉图斯人的一片橡胶园（诚然，那是一片生长在多样树木之间的橡胶园），一位规划者问我：“你觉得这片印尼丛林怎么样？”仿佛他除了随机的绿色什么也看不见。如果不是这种盲视被写入发展政策，它对这个地区的管理仍不会有多大影响。发展组织了国家对自然资源的开发。20世纪60年代末至90年代末，发展指导这种开发时，仿佛发现自然资源的地区从定义上说就是无人居住的。发展把国家划分为二分区域：人口区与自然资源开发区。在人口区，发展管理社群。在自然资源开发区，人无关紧要。发展的目标是把资源弄出来。

In 1975 a national Forestry Law defined all forests as the property of the state, to be used according to state-designated national priorities. Local rights over forested lands were written out of existence. Lots of areas without trees were mapped as “forests”; many towns and villages were included.

Unfortunately for the residents of the Meratus Mountains, and other vast pieces of Indonesia’s Outer Islands, the bureaucrats never consulted them about the definition of “forests.” They just assumed that the whole area was forested. This has meant that the whole area belongs to the state to be used for natural resource exploitation as the state pleases. It has also meant that experts and planners have not been encouraged to recognize the social history of the forest. They are trained specifically to see forests outside of appropriate livelihoods and claims.
People in the forests are outlaws.

1975年，一部国家森林法把所有森林定义为国家财产，按国家指定的优先事项使用。当地对林地的权利被一笔勾销。许多没有树的地区被绘制为“森林”；许多城镇和村庄被包括在内。
对梅拉图斯山脉的居民以及印尼外岛其他广大地区的人来说，不幸的是，官僚从未就“森林”的定义咨询他们。他们只是假定整个地区都是森林。这意味着整个地区属于国家，国家可以随意用于自然资源开发。这也意味着专家和规划者从未被鼓励去认识森林的社会历史。他们受到的专门训练，是把森林看成与正当的生计活动和权利主张无关的地方。
森林中的人是法外之徒。

The effectiveness of this training still presents a puzzle: How can it be so easy to impose official “forests” on social landscapes? To answer I can only point to the cultural legacy of official forests, in which repeated policy enactments each make the category seem more necessary, more reasonable, and more a piece of common sense. National resource policy draws directly on the colonial resource policy of the Netherlands Indies. Colonial policy, in turn, drew its model of rural landscapes in part from pre-colonial kingdoms in Java. Wet-rice fields were the favored landscapes of the court; wet-rice fields symbolized not only a community of stable subjects, but also the order and prosperity that the king could bring to the land. In contrast, the forests beyond were imagined as places of wild animals, fierce bandits, and recalcitrant shifting cultivators: unruly subjects on unruly landscapes (Dove 1985; Day 1994). Colonial administrators borrowed from these courtly aesthetics in imagining the rural landscapes they could best control. The Dutch extended wet-rice cultivation, first across Java and then across the archipelago, settling their subjects properly.

They also imagined new ways to use the wild forest landscapes that Javanese kings despised: These would be the places where natural resources could be freely extracted by European industry. In 1871, an Agrarian Law divided the colony into two types of land: native land and land for European exploitation. Native land would be the site of colonial administration of resident communities; the rest of the colony could be regarded as effectively uninhabited, free for plantations, mines, or other enterprises.
校注5

这种训练的有效性仍然令人费解：把官方“森林”强加于社会地景，怎么会如此容易？要回答，我只能指出官方森林的文化遗产；在反复的政策制定中，这一范畴显得越来越必要、越来越合理、越来越像常识。国家资源政策直接借用荷属东印度的殖民资源政策。殖民政策又把其乡村地景模型部分取自爪哇的前殖民王国。水田是宫廷偏爱的地景；水田不仅象征稳定的臣民共同体，也象征国王能为土地带来的秩序与繁荣。相比之下，更远处的森林被想象为野兽、凶悍盗匪和顽抗的游耕者之地：不驯的臣民住在不驯的地景上（Dove 1985; Day 1994）。殖民行政官借用这些宫廷美学，想象他们最能控制的乡村地景。荷兰人先是在爪哇，继而在整个群岛推广水田耕作，把臣民妥善定居下来。
他们也想象出利用爪哇国王所鄙视的野生森林地景的新方式：这些地方将成为欧洲工业自由开采自然资源的场所。1871年，一部土地法把殖民地分为两类土地：原住民土地与供欧洲人开发的土地。原住民土地将成为殖民行政机构管理居民社群的场所；殖民地的其余部分可以被视为实际上无人居住，任由种植园、矿山或其他企业使用。

After independence, this dualistic division between native and European zones was repudiated in the Indonesian Agrarian Law of 1960; however, it was recapitulated in the passage of the 1975 Forestry Law, which gave all forests to the state for natural resource exploitation. Once again, the country would be divided, as it had been under colonial rule, into zones of human management and zones of resource management. In the latter zones, the claims and livelihoods of local residents would be irrelevant; the ghosts of Javanese pre-colonial courts still called these people unruly, and colonial laws still criminalized them. As natural resource exploitation became a focus of state-building, logging, mining, and tree plantations spread through Kalimantan. Each of these operations required landscapes that were empty of people and their property rights, that is, in national parlance, “forests.” Each drew on the precedence of the others to argue that the forests they found were, by definition, empty and wild. Each stabilized the others’ understanding of forested landscapes as wild places; each made this cultural legacy more obvious-seeming and more real.
校注4

独立后，这种原住民区与欧洲区的二元划分在1960年印尼土地法中被否定；然而，它在1975年森林法通过时又被重演，该法把所有森林交给国家用于自然资源开发。这个国家将再次像殖民统治下那样，被划分为人类管理区与资源管理区。在后者中，当地居民的认领与生计无关紧要；爪哇前殖民宫廷的幽灵仍在称这些人为不驯者，殖民法律仍把他们定为罪犯。随着自然资源开发成为国家建设的焦点，伐木、采矿和树木种植园在加里曼丹蔓延。这些作业每一种都需要没有居民及其产权的地景，用国家话语说，就是“森林”。每一个都援引其他的先例，论证它们所发现的森林从定义上说就是空无而野生的。每一个都稳定了其他方面对森林地景作为荒野之地的理解；每一个都使这份文化遗产显得更明显、更真实。
校注4

Many conservationists have accepted the definition of the rural landscape offered by this legacy without a moment of self-consciousness. To fight for nature reserves and parks, they wrench forest areas away from national development to make way for an equivalently valued national conservation. Conservation forests, like development’s production forests, would contribute to the power of the nation and its elites, at least symbolically. Like developers, these conventional conservationists have seen the forests’ residents as interlopers, bandits, destroyers of the nation’s value. The secondary forests that follow in their wake are the sign of their destructiveness. Caught by the legacy that stretches from Javanese kings to national development, conventional conservationists never look at landscapes—those historical configurations of both nature and society—even as they describe the wild nature that can only be found on those landscapes.

许多保护主义者不加反思地接受了这份遗产所提供的乡村地景定义。为争取自然保护区和公园，他们把森林区域从国家发展中夺走，为同等受重视的国家保护让路。保护林，如同发展中的生产林，至少象征性地为国家及其精英的权力作出贡献。像开发商一样，这些常规保护主义者把森林居民视为闯入者、盗匪、国家价值的破坏者。紧随其后的次生林是他们破坏性的标志。被从爪哇国王延伸到国家发展的这份遗产困住，常规保护主义者从不观看地景——那些自然与社会兼具的历史配置——即使他们在描述只能在这些地景上找到的野生自然。

The Meratus landscape is intelligible to neither developers nor conventional conservationists. It is in this sense that I describe it as forming within a “gap.” Gaps are zones of erasure and incomprehensibility. Gaps occur where metropolitan projects do not reach so far or deep as to change everything according to their plans. Those who believe in evolutionary stories of history try to convince us that gaps are archaic backwaters, left behind the advancing wave of history. People without computers, people without televisions, people without plumbing: Technology, they say, has left them behind. Behind what? How are these discriminations made and maintained? Gaps are always being produced as discriminations are made. Development creates a discrimination between zones of population and zones of resource exploitation; to the extent that the Meratus landscape is made illegible by this discrimination, it occupies a gap. This gap is not a transcendent, transhistorical space of difference. Gaps are only experienced from the perspective of a particular, historically instituted line of demarcation in relation to which certain ways of being seem invalid or illegible. From another perspective, that gap may be another form of ordinariness. Yet some perspectives are more powerful than others. To the extent that categories are drawn with power, the gaps they stimulate are worth taking seriously as critical spaces and sites for emergent voices and dreams.

梅拉图斯地景对开发商和常规保护主义者都不可理解。在这个意义上，我把它描述为在“空白”中形成。空白是抹除与不可理解的区域。空白出现在大都市项目未能抵达那么远、那么深，无法按计划改变一切的地方。相信历史进化故事的人试图让我们相信，空白是古老而停滞的僻壤，被历史前进的浪潮抛在后面。没有电脑的人，没有电视的人，没有给排水设施的人：他们说，技术把他们抛在了后面。抛在什么后面？这些区分是如何作出并维持的？空白总是在区分被作出时产生。发展在人口区与资源开发区之间制造区分；就梅拉图斯地景因这一区分而变得不可辨识而言，它占据了一个空白。这个空白不是超验的、跨历史的差异空间。空白只能从特定、历史性建立的划界视角被经验；相对于这条界线，某些存在方式显得无效或不可读。从另一个视角看，这个空白也许是另一种平常。然而有些视角比另一些更有权力。只要范畴的划定有权力支撑，它们造成的空白就值得被认真视为批判性空间，以及新兴声音与梦想的场所。
It has been easy for me to pick out the gaps that development policy creates because justice-oriented Indonesian environmental activists have picked them out for me.

Taking up the cause of people who live in state-demarcated zones of natural resource exploitation, they have argued that we need to imagine conservation and development differently: The rights of forestliving people must be respected, and their traditional systems of forest management should be maintained. With the demise of the New Order, such criticisms and suggestions may carry some weight. The early twenty-first century is a time of change and ferment in national forest policy, and some NGO models may yet become national law.
我很轻易就挑出了发展政策造成的空白，因为以正义为导向的印尼环保活动家已经替我挑出来了。
他们为生活在国家划定的自然资源开发区中的人民争取权益，论证我们需要以不同方式想象保护与发展：森林居民的权利必须受到尊重，他们传统的森林管理制度应当得到维持。随着新秩序终结，这类批评和建议可能有些分量。21世纪初是国家森林政策变化与发酵的时期，一些非政府组织模式也许终将成为国家法律。

This is a great moment when many things are possible. It is also a moment for reflection. As we redress the gaps of previous ways of seeing, are we developing our own distinctive gaps? What kinds of dialogues between urban policy and rural landscape maintenance are we making possible?
这是一个许多事情都可能发生的伟大时刻。这也是一个反思的时刻。当我们纠正以往观看方式的空白时，我们是否正在形成自己独特的空白？我们正在使城市政策与乡村地景维护之间形成什么样的对话？

Justice-oriented environmental activists, both in Indonesia and internationally, ask us to imagine both conservation and development on a community scale. This is a great starting point. However, sometimes even these plans get caught in the legacy of separation between people and forests. Some of the best-laid environmentalist agendas reproduce the separation of zones of population and zones of resource management, but in miniature: The landscape is imagined as a series of enclosed communities, each with its settlements and fields, on the one hand, and its reserved forests, on the other.

This has many advantages over national development and conservation, but it still makes it difficult to see the forest as a social landscape. Must we always assume a distinction between settlements, as centers of sociability and livelihood, and hinterlands, as zones of resource management? Once again, Meratus landscapes are found only in the gap.
以正义为导向的环保活动家，无论在印尼还是国际上，都要求我们在社群尺度上想象保护与发展。这是一个很好的起点。然而，有时即使这些计划也陷入人与森林分离的遗产。一些筹划得最好的环保议程，以缩微形式复制了人口区与资源管理区的分离：地景被想象为一系列封闭社群，每个社群一边有自己的定居点和田地，另一边有自己的保留森林。
这比国家发展与保护有许多优势，但仍让人难以把森林看作社会地景。我们是否必须总是假定定居地（社会性与生计中心）与腹地（资源管理区）之间的区分？再一次，梅拉图斯地景只在空白中被发现。
Inside the Gap between Settlements and Hinterlands

Consider the shadow communities of the Ayuh River valley. The Ayuh is a great stream that flows through the mountains. Long before it makes its way, at last sluggish, to the coast, it bores through canyons and crashes over falls: It is not a navigation channel to the plains. Instead, its mountain segment cradles a landscape of small swidden clusters surrounded by forest: familiar forest to the people who live there, who have watched and nurtured their scattered fruit and honey trees, discovered favorite hunting and fishing haunts, and retraced the tracks of an older generation’s old swiddens, materialized in enriched forest regrowth. In that landscape lies a set of once and future communities: reminders and possibilities for sociality that shadow contemporary community commitments. The overlapping spheres and tracks of familiar forest are the Ayuh’s shadow communities.
在定居地与腹地之间的空白内部

想想阿尤河谷的影子社群。阿尤河是一条流经群山的大河。在它最终缓缓流向海岸之前，它穿过峡谷，冲下瀑布：它不是通往平原的航道。相反，它的山地段孕育一片地景：被森林环绕的一簇簇小片游耕田。对居住在那里的人来说，这是熟悉的森林；他们照看并培育散落的果树和蜜树，发现喜爱的狩猎和捕鱼地点，追溯老一代旧刀耕火种田的轨迹——这些轨迹物化为丰富的再生林。那片地景中有一组曾经与未来的社群：它们是社会性的提醒与可能性，为当代的社群承诺投下影子。熟悉森林重叠的领域与轨迹，就是阿尤河的影子社群。

“Community” here means sharing food, work, and ceremony. In one of its most formal instantiations, game and big fish are divided into cubes and counted out in piles to be distributed to each household. Rice planting is done in a large group gathered through reciprocal labor exchange. The ceremony that makes newly harvested rice fit to eat gathers everyone in a great celebration. Each of these makes a named “community” real. Yet throughout the Meratus Mountains communities are flexibly reconstructed in constant negotiations. This globally common feature of social life is particularly self-evident in the central mountains, where houses are widely separated, perched adjacent to swidden fields. Households are free to affiliate with neighbors in different directions, coalescing ever-changing communities. In a year or two they make a new house and a new swidden, and, in the process, forge a new set of social ties that may replicate or transform last year’s commitments. Nowhere is this more evident than in the forests along the Ayuh River.

这里的“社群”意味着分享食物、劳动和仪式。在最正式的一种具体形式中，猎物和大鱼被切成方块，分成堆计数，分配给每一户。播种稻谷由一大群人完成，他们通过互惠换工聚集起来。使新收稻米适合食用的仪式，把所有人聚集在一场盛大庆祝中。每一项都使一个被命名的“社群”成为真实。然而在整个梅拉图斯山脉，社群在不断协商中被灵活地重建。这一全球常见的社会生活特征在中部山区尤其不言自明：房屋相隔很远，坐落在刀耕火种田旁。家庭可以自由地与不同方向的邻居结盟，聚合成不断变化的社群。一两年后，他们建一座新房子、开一片新田，并在此过程中缔结一套新的社会纽带，这些纽带可能复制或改变去年的承诺。这一点在阿尤河沿岸的森林中最为明显。

Because the Ayuh River is not a path to the coast, households along it orient themselves, in part, along other paths: the trails that cross the mountain divide on either side, leading to market towns and government centers. These trails are various, following the Ayuh’s many tributaries up into the mountains and over passes before descending into the surrounding plains. Men hike these trails to bring forest products and crops to market; they hike back with news of products, prices, and politics. They visit kin and friends who live along these trails; they find potential spouses, political allies, and new styles and stories all along the way. Orientation to these various “exits” splinter the connections among Ayuh valley households, pulling them centrifugally into the social networks along these tributaries. Ayuh River communities are unstable, contested, and constantly breaking up and reforming.

由于阿尤河不是通往海岸的道路，沿岸家庭部分地沿着其他路径定位自己：那些穿越两侧山脊、通往集镇和政府中心的小径。这些小径多种多样，沿阿尤河的许多支流上山，越过山口，再下到周围平原。男人们沿这些小径徒步，把林产品和作物带到市场；他们带着关于产品、价格和政治的消息徒步回来。他们拜访沿这些小径居住的亲戚和朋友；一路上，他们找到潜在配偶、政治盟友，以及新的风格和故事。对这些不同“出口”的取向，使阿尤河谷家庭之间的联系碎裂，把他们离心式地拉入这些支流沿岸的社会网络。阿尤河社群不稳定、有争议，并不断破裂和重组。
Individual households that farm along the Ayuh one year are likely to move up a tributary for next year’s farm, joining the people there.
今年在阿尤河沿岸务农的个别家庭，明年很可能沿一条支流上移，加入那里的人，去开垦明年的农田。

Yet the lands around the Ayuh River are a good place to farm, fish, and hunt, and, any given year, there are quite a few people living there. These people have some of their familiar forests along the Ayuh stream. Familiar forests are always in process, changing as new trees are planted and claimed, new routes for forest collection found, new swiddens cut and old ones eased back into forest. Familiar forests always overlap. Any time a group of households agrees to make adjacent swiddens, they have affirmed at least one future site of overlapping familiarity: the regrowing forest that replaces their swiddens. The more formal claims of named communities are possible because they map on to at least one segment of each constituent household’s familiar forest. Next year, each constituent household may choose whether or not to continue its membership in that community; all it has to do is move or reach out to a different segment of its familiar forest to affiliate with another community.

然而阿尤河周围的土地是务农、捕鱼和打猎的好地方，而且任何一年都有相当多的人住在那里。这些人在阿尤河沿岸拥有一些熟悉的森林。熟悉的森林始终处于过程之中，随着新树被栽种和认领、新的森林采集路线被发现、新的刀耕火种田被开垦、旧田慢慢回归森林而变化。熟悉的森林总是重叠。每当一群家庭同意开垦相邻的田，他们至少确认了一个未来重叠熟悉的地点：取代他们田地的再生林。被命名社群的较正式认领之所以可能，是因为它们至少对应每个组成家庭熟悉森林的一个片段。明年，每个组成家庭都可以选择是否继续留在那个社群中；它所要做的，只是搬迁，或把联系延伸到熟悉森林的另一片区域，与另一个社群结盟。

The forest is full of the markings of past communities, and these are also potential communities. An island of fruit trees in the forest marks a past swidden cluster. The site of an old ritual hall is remembered as a once and future community center, even as the site has blended into surrounding forest. People are reminded of these nodes of sociality every time they look at the vegetation and recall its social history. People use the stories of these shadow communities to negotiate current social responsibilities: to kindle companionship, to solicit assistance with tasks, or to find allies.
森林里满是以往社群的标记，而这些也是潜在的社群。森林中一片果树之岛，标记着过去的一组游耕田。一座旧仪式厅的遗址被记忆为曾经与未来的社群中心，即使该地已融入周围森林。人们每次看到植被、回想起它的社会历史，就会想起这些社会性节点。人们用这些影子社群的故事来协商当前的社会责任：点燃友谊，请求帮忙完成任务，或寻找盟友。

I first became aware of these shadow communities when I was living with a household on the Ayuh River. A man came by whose current home was many hours’ hike upstream. He was visiting a man in my household about a local political matter, a contested marriage. To demonstrate his closeness to his host, he evoked their common membership in a community I had never heard of. It turned out to be a community that had broken apart about thirty years before. The community “center” the men identified—at a point between their current locations—was long grown up in forest. Yet it was still clearly marked in the forest vegetation; they knew it every time they passed that way. Encouraged by this material presence, our visitor claimed for this shadow community both a territory and a constituency. He talked me through a sketch map of this territory: No matter that it borrowed segments from four contemporary communities; this was a community that still existed, in shadow form, in the evidence of the forest. Made from overlapping familiar forests, and read from forest histories, communities in the Ayuh valley are simultaneously fragile and persistent, overlaid yet allowing discrete claims, composed of natural forest and of social settlement.

我第一次意识到这些影子社群，是在阿尤河沿岸与一户人家同住时。一个男人来访，他现在的家在上游数小时徒步路程之外。他来与我同住的这户人家的一个男人谈一件当地政治事务，一桩有争议的婚姻。为表明与主人的亲近，他提起他们共同属于一个我从未听说过的社群。结果那是一个大约三十年前就已散掉的社群。两人所指的社群“中心”——位于他们现在住处之间的某处——早已长成森林。但它在森林植被中仍清晰可辨；每次经过那里，他们都知道。受这种物质存在的鼓励，我们的访客为这个影子社群同时主张一片领土和一个成员群。他边讲解，边引导我画出这片领土的草图：尽管它从四个当代社群借用了片段，却无关紧要；这是一个仍然存在的社群，以影子形式存在于森林的证据中。阿尤河谷的社群由重叠的熟悉森林构成，并从森林历史中读取，因而既脆弱又持久，彼此覆盖，却又允许分离的认领，由天然森林与社会定居共同组成。

Even where communities have more geographic grounds for stability, the importance of familiar forests in composing them allows them to stretch, split, and change their shape like amoebae. Individuals and groups bud off. Without ever leaving their own familiar forests, households may turn in another direction, away from the community’s current focal point to join another community’s social networks.
即使社群有更多地理基础来保持稳定，熟悉森林在构成社群中的重要性，仍使它们能像变形虫一样伸展、分裂、改变形状。个人和群体出芽分离。家庭从未离开自己的熟悉森林，却可以转向另一个方向，离开社群当前的中心，加入另一个社群的社会网络。

All of this makes it very difficult to tell the difference between settlements and hinterlands in the central mountains. Yet community leaders do their best to misrepresent this situation to regional administrators and development experts. Ambitious for their own recognition, leaders portray Meratus communities in terms that outsiders can understand. They claim distinctive community centers and fixed territories; this keeps their communities on administrators’ maps. These are more than idle claims: Leaders do their best to make administrators’ categories come to life on the ground, at least in tentative performances of appropriate behavior. But, in the central Meratus Mountains, they have been unable to change the daily practices of landscape-making that allow their neighbors to reaffiliate, move apart, and choose their own livelihood trajectories.

这一切使中部山区的定居地与腹地之间的区别很难分辨。然而社群领袖竭力向地区行政官员和发展专家不实地呈现这种情况。为了自己得到承认，领袖们用外来者能理解的话语描绘梅拉图斯社群。他们主张独特的社群中心和固定领土；这使他们的社群留在行政官员的地图上。这些并非空口主张：领袖们尽力让行政官员的范畴在实地活起来，至少以尝试性的合宜行为表演来体现。但在中梅拉图斯山脉，他们未能改变地景制造的日常实践，而正是这些实践让邻居们能够重新结盟、迁离，并选择自己的生计轨迹。

By the 1990s, conservation had become a small, if growing, outside authority in the Meratus Mountains. Some Meratus leaders learned the rhetoric of conservation, and they learned to produce its performances: They planned ecotourism and spoke of traditional benevolence toward the spirits of plants and animals; they showed outsiders their reserved forests. As with development, it was not always clear whether even the close kin and neighbors of these accomplished leaders shared their enthusiasm about these performances. Leadership claims and commitments had a minimal effect on most people’s daily life projects, and on the landscape. Once again, a bad basis for dialogue was developing.
到20世纪90年代，保护已成为梅拉图斯山脉一种虽小却不断增长的外部权威。一些梅拉图斯领袖学会了保护修辞，也学会了生产其表演：他们规划生态旅游，谈论对动植物精灵的传统仁慈；他们向外来者展示自己的保留森林。与发展一样，甚至这些有成就的领袖的近亲和邻居，也未必都对这些表演抱有同样的热情。领导权主张和承诺对大多数人的日常生活计划以及地景影响甚微。再一次，一个糟糕的对话基础正在形成。

Yet many of the conservationists who visit the Meratus Mountains are committed to empowering Meratus through community-based conservation. Why might this basically great idea create some of the same troubled dynamics as militarized and corrupt development policies? Advocates are pushed into much the same position as Meratus community leaders: If they do not portray resources and communities in terms that are recognizable by the state, national elites, and international experts, their advocacy will be entirely ineffective. In this context, advocates represent rural communities in ways that are the opposite of their audiences’ worst fears: The people, they say, are organized into obedient communities with a clear structure of leadership, rational management policies, and clearly bounded territories. All that remains is to offer these communities rights.

然而，访问梅拉图斯山脉的许多保护主义者，都致力于通过以社区为基础的保护来赋权梅拉图斯人。为什么这个基本上很好的想法，会造成一些与军事化和腐败的发展政策相同的有问题的动态？倡导者被推到与梅拉图斯社群领袖大致相同的位置：如果他们不用国家、国家精英和国际专家可识别的话语来描绘资源与社群，他们的倡导就完全无效。在这种背景下，倡导者以与其受众最深恐惧相反的方式来表现乡村社群：他们说，这些人被组织成服从的社群，有清晰的领导结构、合理的管理政策和明确划定的领土。剩下要做的，就是给予这些社群权利。

As advocacy this is proper and important, even with its assumptions: a unified and stable community; clearly stated management plans; and traditional customary territory. I don’t think advocates are able to operate without winning images and frameworks. Yet perhaps there is some room here to maneuver—and room to learn.
作为倡导，这是恰当而重要的，即使带有这些假设：一个统一稳定的社群；明确陈述的管理计划；传统习惯领土。我不认为倡导者能在没有有吸引力的形象和框架的情况下运作。不过，这里也许还有一些回旋余地——也有学习余地。

And so, I emphasize again the practices that link humans and nonhumans in creating the social-natural landscape. Practices show us how landscape biodiversity is materially appreciated; they lead us to questions about particular human-nonhuman relationships and away from barren debates about the wisdom or stupidity of primitive people. Instead of basing rights claims on equivalents to private property, we might train our vision on the overlapping socialities of familiar forests, as these empower and constrain individuals in using forest resources. For example, even planted Meratus trees of any stature have multiple claimants: the descendants, male and female, of the original planter. No claimant can expect to profit from the tree alone. Forest management is facilitated, not hampered, by such overlapping and diverse claims (for example, rights to share in the product; see Tsing 2003a). Overlapping claims are a form of “community” through which forests are maintained. Interspecies socialities are embedded in the forest landscape. Processes of forging human-nonhuman relationships within dynamic, changing forests are as important here as forest boundaries.

因此，我再次强调在创造社会—自然地景中连接人与非人的实践。实践向我们展示地景生物多样性如何在具体的物质实践中受到重视；它们把我们引向关于特定人类—非人类关系的问题，远离关于原始人智慧或愚蠢的贫瘠辩论。与其把权利主张建立在等同于私有财产的基础上，我们也许可以把目光训练到熟悉森林重叠的社会性上，因为这些社会性赋权并约束个人使用森林资源。例如，即使是梅拉图斯人栽种的稍成规模的树木，也有多个认领者：原栽种者的男女后代。任何认领者都不能指望独享树木的收益。这种重叠而多样的认领（例如分享产品的权利；见 Tsing 2003a）促进而非阻碍森林管理。重叠的认领是一种“社群”形式，森林通过它得到维护。跨物种社会性嵌入森林地景之中。在动态变化的森林中锻造人类—非人类关系的过程，在这里与森林边界同样重要。
Landscape and Memory
地景与记忆

The Meratus forest is full of named locations. If Meratus do not lose themselves too often in the forest, it is not because they have a spiritual gift of navigation, as some romantics have claimed, but rather because they orient themselves to known places. Ridges, peaks, and saddles have names, as do prominent rocks and even insignificant creeks and springs and the distinctive pools, falls, and confluences of rivers. Many big trees also have names, that is, not only names for the kind of tree but also individual, personal names. Hillsides are commonly referred to in relation to the name of a big tree. Through these markers, hikers learn their way in the forest and, later, craft their tales of places and events.

梅拉图斯森林里到处是命名地点。如果梅拉图斯人不太常在森林中迷路，并非因为如某些浪漫主义者所称，他们有导航的灵性天赋，而是因为他们以已知地点来定位自己。山脊、山峰和鞍部都有名字，突出的岩石、甚至不起眼的小溪和泉眼，以及河流独特的深潭、瀑布和汇流处也都有名字。许多大树也有名字，不只是树种名称，还有个体的专名。山坡通常借助一棵大树的名称来指称。通过这些标记，徒步者学会在森林中认路，并在后来编织关于地点和事件的故事。

Forest regrowth also orients the hiker: It tells the story of past swiddens as well as forest management. Even without knowing the people who once lived there, Meratus hikers learn something of the social history of the forest through observing the forest regrowth. In their own familiar forests, this regrowth is a place of memory, whether of one’s own past or that of one’s kin and neighbors. Hiking through familiar secondary forest, we often spoke of the stories from the past that forest regrowth told. Even relaxing at home, Meratus are likely to tell stories of their own pasts in relation to the sites they made swiddens as well as the places they traveled. The landscape becomes a medium for telling stories of oneself and others. At one point, I collected “swidden biographies,” that is, narrations of the consecutive swidden sites of each household. Since old swidden sites are not exclusive property claims, I found myself surprised at how easily their sites—and sights—rolled off people’s tongues.
They were easy to tell because the narration of personal history through landscape has been an ordinary genre for speaking about one’s past.

森林再生也为徒步者定向：它讲述过去刀耕火种田以及森林管理的故事。即使不认识曾在那里居住的人，梅拉图斯徒步者也能通过观察森林再生，了解森林社会历史的一些东西。在他们自己熟悉的森林中，这种再生是记忆之地，无论记忆的是自己的过去，还是亲属和邻居的过去。徒步穿过熟悉的次生林时，我们常常谈起森林再生所讲述的往昔故事。即使在家休息，梅拉图斯人也可能讲述自己过去的故事，既涉及他们开垦刀耕火种田的地点，也涉及他们旅行过的地方。地景成为讲述自己与他人故事的媒介。有一段时间，我收集“刀耕火种传记”，即每户家庭连续刀耕火种地点的叙述。既然旧刀耕火种地点并非排他性财产认领，我惊讶地发现，他们的地点——以及景象——如此轻易地脱口而出。
它们容易讲述，是因为通过地景叙述个人历史，一直是谈论自己过去的普通体裁。

Habits of attentiveness, practices of naming, and genres of telling make the forest intelligible for its Meratus residents. The forest appears neither particularly frightening nor wild; it is not outside the bounds of history and civility. Once one considers the possibilities of this kind of forest intelligibility, it seems likely that people all over the world must have come to know forests as social, historical, biographical spaces. How is it that this has been so hard to recognize? What work has it taken to repress the social intelligibility of the forest? These questions bring us back to habits of thinking about nature as global and transcendent, and why these habits have traveled anywhere at all, even if they have not reordered the landscape of the Meratus Mountains.

关注的习惯、命名的实践和讲述的体裁，使森林对梅拉图斯居民来说可理解。森林既不特别可怕，也不特别野性；它并未超出历史与文明的界限。一旦考虑这种森林可理解性的可能，全世界的人想必都曾把森林认识为社会性、历史性、传记性的空间。为何这一点如此难以被承认？压抑森林社会可理解性，需要付出什么样的工作？这些问题把我们带回把自然视为全球性和超越性的思维习惯，以及这些习惯为何能传播到任何地方，即使它们并未重新安排梅拉图斯山脉的地景。
One might again recall how hard European states had to work to evict peasants from their forests.

Only by seizing the forests for elites, thus making forests, coercively, off-limits for peasant uses, did European forests become empty and wild. In this state they could be what one literary critic calls “the shadow of civilization,” that is, nonsocial spaces that haunted European sociality (Harrison 1992). The histories and prehistories of nationalism inscribed in European forests that Simon Schama (1995) tells in delineating a distinctly European set of regimes of “landscape and memory” require forests that have already been claimed for the shadows of nationalist elite imaginations.
人们可以再次回想，欧洲国家曾费多大力气，才把农民逐出他们的森林。
只有为精英夺取森林，从而强行禁止农民使用森林，欧洲森林才变得空无而野生。在这种状态下，它们才能成为一位文学批评家所谓的“文明的影子”，即萦绕欧洲社会性的非社会空间（Harrison 1992）。西蒙·沙玛（1995）在勾勒一套独特的欧洲“地景与记忆”体制时讲述的、铭刻在欧洲森林中的民族主义历史与史前史，以森林已被纳入民族主义精英想象中的阴影领域为前提。

This notion of forests as empty, wild, and available for elite manipulation also formed part of the repertoire of colonial scientists in their quest to understand the environment at the peripheries of European empire (Grove 1995). Forests were a key component of the discovery of this environmental form of “nature,” which, these scientists learned, could be used for European profit but also destroyed beyond repair. They watched European settlers cut down forests; they worried about erosion, loss of species, and climate change. But their attention both to the settlers’ use of forests and to forest protection assumed forests that were outside of long-term social occupation. These could not be forests that formed social “homes” because then they would be available for neither profit nor protection. They learned to observe empty forests, spaces of a nonsocial nature.

森林作为空无、野生且可供精英操纵的观念，也构成殖民科学家在试图理解欧洲帝国边缘环境时所用的一套观念的一部分（Grove 1995）。森林是发现这种环境形式“自然”的关键组成部分；这些科学家得知，这种自然可用于欧洲的利润，但也可能被毁得无法修复。他们看着欧洲定居者砍伐森林；他们担忧侵蚀、物种丧失和气候变化。但他们既关注定居者对森林的使用，也关注森林保护，其前提都是森林处在长期社会占用之外。这些森林不能是形成社会“家园”的森林，因为那样它们就既不能用于利润，也不能用于保护。他们学会观察空无的森林，即非社会自然的空间。

Learning both with and against the natives whose territories they had come to occupy, colonial scientists concluded that this profitable-yet-fragile nature was transcendent, beyond the circumscribed knowledge of any given vernacular culture. Writing to each other from one imperial corner to another, they found that this universal nature was also global, that is, interconnected across the planet. The discourse on deforestation—as necessary to human enterprise yet a cause of systematic environmental deterioration—formed a centerpiece of this discussion of a “nature” that could travel across cultures and across empires.
殖民科学家与他们前来占领其领土的原住民既合作又对抗地学习，得出结论：这种既有利润又脆弱的自然具有超越性，超出任何特定地方性文化有限的知识。他们从一个帝国角落写信给另一个帝国角落，发现这种普遍自然也是全球性的，即在整个星球上相互联系。关于森林砍伐的话语——它既是人类事业所必需，又造成系统的环境退化——成为这场关于一种能跨越文化、跨越帝国传播的“自然”讨论的核心。

When this imperial discourse spread in the twentieth century to inform international development and conservation expertise, the central place of forests was not disturbed. Yet these “forests” are a very particular object, inherited from European state-making and empire-building. Forests are recognizable around the world only to the extent that they are empty and wild, the shadows of civilization. Where indigenous people are recognized within them, international discussion makes the people wild things too, assimilated to the wild emptiness of the forest. Their social lives come out to meet the international public only across a deep abyss; they flit through the forest like birds. In contrast, a more recognizable set of rural people is known in the forest, but as a destructive force: poor peasants. Represented as just ordinary folks, poor people are said to destroy the forest to make their meager living. Third World elites blame them to explain why the forests are disappearing. One sees here the resiliency of the concept of nonsocial forests. If forests are being destroyed, it is society; if they aren’t, it is nature: Everything can be explained by placing it somewhere in the dichotomy of social and natural.

当这种帝国话语在20世纪传播开来，为国际发展与保护专业知识提供信息时，森林的中心地位并未受到扰乱。然而这些“森林”是一个非常特殊的对象，继承自欧洲的国家建构与帝国建设。森林只有在空无而野生、作为文明之影的程度上，才在世界各地被识别。当原住民在其中被承认时，国际讨论也把人变成野性之物，同化于森林的野生空无。他们的社会生活只有跨越一道深渊才出来与国际公众相见；他们像鸟一样掠过森林。相比之下，一类更容易辨识的乡村人群在森林中为人所知，却是作为破坏性力量：贫穷农民。穷人被表现为普通百姓，据说是为了维持微薄生计而毁坏森林。第三世界精英责备他们，以解释森林为何正在消失。在此可见非社会森林概念的韧性。如果森林正被摧毁，那是社会；如果没有，那是自然：只要把一切放进社会与自然的二分法，就都能解释。

The Meratus Mountains have not escaped the gaze stimulated by this framework, but rather are repeatedly inscribed. The Social Welfare Department saw “social” people destroying “natural” forests and tried to resettle the people out of the forests. The loggers saw empty, natural forest and came in to log it. The plantation operators saw forest degraded by society and needing to be restored to nature—in a monocrop, profitable form. I could continue. But this is not everything that is going on. There are other forests here too: the social-natural forests of Meratus residents. To see these forests, a change in perspective is required. I mark this change of perspective in the idea of “gaps.” Gaps develop in the seams of universal projects; they are found where universals have not been successful in setting all the terms. While a transcendent, nonsocial, global “nature” has become a powerful thing worldwide, it is not the only kind of nature on the planet. Whenever we want to trace the limits of hegemony, we need to look for gaps. An ethnography of global connection is impossible without this tool.

梅拉图斯山脉并未逃脱这一框架所激发的凝视，反而被反复铭写。社会福利部看到“社会性”的人在毁坏“天然”森林，试图把人迁出森林重新安置。伐木者看到空无的天然森林，进来采伐。种植园经营者看到因社会活动而退化的森林，需要恢复为自然——以单一作物、有利可图的形式。我可以继续列举。但这不是事情的全部。这里还有别的森林：梅拉图斯居民的社会—自然森林。要看见这些森林，需要改变视角。我用“空白”这一观念标记这种视角变化。空白在普遍工程的接缝中发展；它们出现在普遍物未能成功设定所有条件的地方。虽然一种超越的、非社会的、全球的“自然”已成为世界上强大的事物，但它不是地球上唯一的自然。每当我们想追踪霸权的局限，就需要寻找空白。没有这一工具，全球联结的民族志不可能完成。

en: The flexibility of the concept of “planting” is suggested by the way tree claims are tied to the whole range of ways, from deliberate to casual, of sprouting the tree. A Meratus who threw a durian seed out the door of her house while eating the fruit would never describe herself as “planting.” However, if the seed sprouted and grew, she would claim the tree as one of her planting, because of its timing and location next to her house. Fruit trees that sprouted in the area of someone's current house or swidden were always claimed by the householders as their trees unless they were planted with some ceremony by someone else (as, for example, when I was invited to plant durian for when I came back).
zh: “种植”这一概念的灵活性，体现在树木所有权主张与各种使树发芽的方式——从刻意到随意——之间的联系上。一个梅拉图斯人在吃榴莲时把种子从家门扔出去，绝不会说自己在“种植”。然而，如果种子发芽生长，她就会主张这棵树是自己种植的，因为它发芽的时间与她居住于此的时期吻合，而且位置就在她家旁边。在某人现在的房屋或刀耕火种地范围内发芽的果树，除非是别人以某种仪式种下的（例如，我曾被邀请种下一棵榴莲树，以备我将来回来时享用），否则总是被住户声称为自己的树。

en: There are many kinds of huyi, each with long, flexible stems that are good for tying and weaving. Huyi lamab and huyi lantau are used for tying posts and bamboo walkways. Huyi galang and huyi irit are also good for tying; before the market was homogenized, they had good market value. Huyi lilin, “waxy rattan,” is a fine-stemmed rattan used whole, rather than split, to tie house floors. Huyi kaningai is similar, but it is only found in wet mountain saddles, in the kind of forest called gunungan. Huyi karas, “hard rattan,” has a more brittle stem. Huyi wariung is a dark-stemmed rattan with excellent weaving qualities; it makes the most durable back-baskets. Huyi dabanan is the stiffest of the rattans called huyi; it makes superior spear handles. There are also many rattans not classified as huyi, such as nangi, pikak, and ariwa.
zh: huyi 有许多种类，每一种都有长而柔韧的茎，适合捆扎和编织。Huyi lamab 和 huyi lantau 用于捆扎柱子和竹道。Huyi galang 和 huyi irit 也适合捆扎；在市场同质化之前，它们有很好的市场价值。Huyi lilin（“蜡藤”）是一种细茎藤，整根使用而不劈开，用来捆扎房屋地板。Huyi kaningai 类似，但只见于潮湿的山鞍部，生长在称为 gunungan 的那种森林中。Huyi karas（“硬藤”）的茎更脆。Huyi wariung 是一种深色茎的藤，编织性能极佳；它做成的背篓最为耐用。Huyi dabanan 是所有称为 huyi 的藤中最硬的；它做成的矛柄最为优良。还有许多藤类不被归为 huyi，例如 nangi、pikak 和 ariwa。

en: E. P. Thompson (1975) describes the harsh laws created in England to enclose the forests, keeping out peasant “poachers.” In a similar spirit, Peter Sahlins ( 1994) describes the resistance of French peasants to the exclusivity of state and industrial forest claims. Nor were such enclosures limited to Europe: Gold and Gujar (2002) tell how royalty in Rajastan claimed exclusive privilege over the forest; as soon as the king was deposed, peasants flocked into these royal spaces, destroying them. The willingness of peasants to destroy forests leads many analysts to conclude that forest users cannot conserve. Yet this conclusion ignores the political history of elite expropriation, in which peasants and forests became pitted against each other.
zh: E. P. Thompson（1975）描述了英国为圈占森林、排斥农民“偷猎者”而制定的严苛法律。Peter Sahlins（1994）以类似精神描述了法国农民对国家与工业森林主张之排他性的抵抗。这种圈占也不限于欧洲：Gold 和 Gujar（2002）讲述了拉贾斯坦的王室如何声称对森林拥有专有特权；国王一被废黜，农民便涌入这些王室空间并将其毁坏。农民毁林的意愿使许多分析者断定，森林使用者无法保护森林。然而，这一结论忽略了精英剥夺的政治史——在其中，农民与森林被置于彼此对立的位置。
